problem_statement:
Ordering problem in admin RelatedFieldListFilter and RelatedOnlyFieldListFilter

Description

The RelatedFieldListFilter does not fall back to the ordering defined in a model's Meta.ordering. Ordering gets set to an empty tuple in the admin filters implementation (django/contrib/admin/filters.py at the site of the file that initializes the filter), and unless ordering is defined on the related model's ModelAdmin class it remains an empty tuple. It should instead fall back to the ordering defined on the related model's Meta.ordering.

The RelatedOnlyFieldListFilter does not apply any ordering to the related model at all, even when ordering is defined on the related model's ModelAdmin class. This happens because the call to the field's get_choices method omits the ordering keyword argument entirely (in the same admin filters implementation, at the location where choices are retrieved).

problem_statement:
Allow cleaned_data to overwrite fields' default values.
Description

See comments here: https://github.com/django/django/pull/7068/files#r289432409

Currently, when submitting a form, if some_field is not present in the submitted data payload (for example, it wasn't included in the form because its value is derived from another field), and that field has a default value defined on the model, the default cannot be overwritten by assigning a value in cleaned_data. This behavior breaks the expected paradigm where data can be modified in cleaned_data during form processing. Instead, it forces the developer to copy values into and overwrite the raw submitted data.

 class ModelBackendTest(BaseModelBackendTest, TestCase):
     """
problem_statement:
Title: ModelBackend.authenticate() shouldn't make a database query when username is None

Description

I find it easier to explain the issue by describing the current implementation of ModelBackend.authenticate(). When the method is called, if the username parameter is missing it is taken from the keyword arguments using the user model's configured username field. The code then notes that at this point both username and password can be missing (typically when credentials are provided for another backend). Despite that, the implementation continues and performs a user lookup in the database by the username. If the lookup fails, the code runs the default password hasher once by creating a fresh user model instance and hashing the provided password to reduce timing differences between existing and nonexistent users. Otherwise it proceeds to handle the found user.

My suggestion is to short-circuit earlier: if username is missing or password is missing, immediately return without doing a lookup or hashing.

I noticed this when writing assertNumQueries tests in django-sesame, which provides another authentication backend. In those tests I observed that a SQL query was executed which selected user fields from the auth_user table with a WHERE clause that matched rows where username is NULL, and the query had no parameters. That query doesn't make sense because the username column is not nullable.

I considered the timing concern: authenticate tries to mask timing differences between existing and non-existing users by doing a dummy hash when the user doesn't exist. However, I don't think that timing concern should extend across different authentication backends, since different backends run different code paths and will naturally have timing differences. In the scenario I'm describing, callers are currently paying the time cost of performing the dummy password hash and then the time cost of the other authentication backend, which creates a timing difference. With the change I propose, callers would only pay the time cost of their other authentication backend.

problem_statement:
The URL translation function creates an incorrect URL when optional named groups are missing in the URL pattern.

Description

There is a problem when translating URLs with absent 'optional' arguments (this is demonstrated by a test case included with the patch).
hints_text:
Could you please provide the patch as a pull request against master? Unless this is a regression, it probably doesn't qualify for a backport to 1.9 (see our ​supported versions policy). Please check the patch on Python 3 as well (dict.iteritems() doesn't exist there).
The issue here is that resolve() will return None for any optional capture groups that aren't captured, but reverse() will use force_text() and convert it to the literal string 'None'. This causes an asymmetry between resolve() and reverse(). I think it's a better idea to treat this asymmetry as a bug, and solve it within reverse(). We would discard any arguments that are None. Incidentally this will allow for cleaner code when you don't know if an optional parameter is set when you call reverse() or the {% url %} template tag: {% if obj.might_be_none != None %} {% url 'my_view' obj.might_be_none %} {% else %} {% url 'my_view' %} {% endif %} vs. {% url 'my_view' obj.might_be_none %} I think that's a reasonably common usecase, so it would be nice to support this cleaner syntax. Non-existent template variables will still pass an empty string rather than None, so this won't hide any typos in your template variable names.
This also affects the set_language function. When changing language on a page with an URL pattern containing an optional group, the empty optional part is set to none and translating the page leads to a 404. The bug on translation did not exist back in 1.8, not sure when it was introduced. I'm on 2.2. The best way to resolve both issues would be to patch directly _reverse_with_prefix in django.urls.resolvers.

problem_statement:
Composed queries cannot change the list of columns with values()/values_list().

Description

When a composed QuerySet is evaluated multiple times using values() or values_list(), it is not possible to change which columns are returned between evaluations. For example: a ReservedName record is created with name equal to 'a' and order equal to 2. A QuerySet qs1 is obtained from ReservedName.objects.all(), and a union of qs1 with itself is created. Evaluating values_list while requesting the columns name and order returns a tuple containing 'a' and 2. Evaluating values_list again on the same composed QuerySet but requesting only the order column unexpectedly still returns the tuple containing both 'a' and 2. See compiler.py#L428-L433.

problem_statement:
Title
Email messages crash on non-ASCII domain when email encoding is non-unicode.

Description
When the computer hostname is set to a unicode string (in my case the characters for "正宗"), a mail test fails. Because the email encoding is set to iso-8859-1, Python attempts to convert all of the headers to that encoding, including the Message-ID header which Django sets when constructing the message. This is not just a problem in the tests — Django should be handling message encoding more robustly.

Steps to recreate
- Set the system hostname to a value that is not representable in iso-8859-1 (for example, use the unicode characters "正宗").
- Run the mail test suite.

Observed behavior
When encoding is iso-8859-1, the header generation attempts to encode the Message-ID (which contains the hostname) using that single-byte encoding and fails.

Fix
Have django.core.mail.utils or django.core.mail.message convert domain names to punycode before using them in Message-ID and other headers.

Test (described)
A unit test patches the DNS_NAME used for Message-ID generation to a value consisting of non-ASCII characters. It then creates an EmailMessage, sets its encoding to iso-8859-1, generates the MIME message, and asserts that the generated Message-ID contains the punycode form of the domain (i.e., that the non-ASCII domain was converted to punycode before being included in headers).

Affected areas / APIs
- Message-ID header generation in django.core.mail.message
- Domain name source (DNS_NAME) used for make_msgid
- Header handling that enforces single-line headers and encodes values when an explicit message encoding is set

Error messages observed
- UnicodeEncodeError: 'ascii' codec can't encode characters in position 39-40: ordinal not in range(128)
- UnicodeEncodeError: 'latin-1' codec can't encode characters in position 39-40: ordinal not in range(256)

Additional notes
The core issue is that header value handling tries to encode the entire header using the message encoding, but a non-ASCII domain name should be converted to a transfer-friendly form (punycode) before being inserted into headers so that subsequent ascii or single-byte encodings do not fail.

problem_statement:
Title: admin.E108 is raised on fields accessible only via instance.

Description

As part of startup Django validates the ModelAdmin's list_display list/tuple for correctness (django.admin.contrib.checks._check_list_display). Having upgraded Django from 2.0.7 to 2.2.1 I found that a ModelAdmin with a list_display that used to pass the checks and work fine in the admin now fails validation, preventing Django from starting. A PositionField from the django-positions library triggers this bug; an explanation follows.

Example setup (described rather than shown as code):
- There is a model named Thing with two fields: an integer field named number with default 0, and a PositionField named order.
- There is a ModelAdmin registered for Thing with its list_display containing the strings "number" and "order".

Under Django 2.2.1 this raises an incorrect admin.E108 message saying "The value of list_display[1] refers to 'order' which is not a callable...". Under 2.0.7 Django starts up successfully. If you change the field names so that they are not present (for example renaming "number" to "no_number" or "order" to "no_order") then the validation correctly complains about those missing attributes.

Root cause analysis
The reason for this bug is a particular commit referenced above which was proposed and accepted as a fix for another bug (ticket 28490). While that change fixed the original issue, it broke the functionality of the _check_list_display_item routine in other cases.

The rationale for the commit was that after calling getattr(model, item) the result could be None if the attribute was a descriptor returning None, but subsequent code incorrectly interpreted a None result as if getattr had raised AttributeError. The commit attempted to address that conflation. However, because that change introduced an early check that relied on hasattr(model, item), in some cases we no longer attempt to retrieve the field via the model meta API (model._meta.get_field(item)) before returning an error. For PositionField the problem occurs because the descriptor's get method raises an exception when called on the PositionField class object (i.e. the field object on the model class) rather than on a model instance, which causes hasattr(model, item) to return False and prevent the later, correct attempt to find the field via model._meta.get_field(item).

Logical cases the check needs to handle
The _check_list_display_item helper needs to consider several different situations:
- Whether the list_display entry is a callable, an attribute on the ModelAdmin, or a string referring to a model attribute/method.
- Whether getattr(model, item) succeeds and returns something (possibly None), or raises.
- Whether model._meta.get_field(item) returns a field, raises FieldDoesNotExist, or returns a ManyToManyField.
- Whether the obtained field value is None (which was the subject of the earlier bug).

Before the offending change, after trying getattr and get_field, the code handled these cases such that:
- If get_field succeeded and the field was not a ManyToManyField, no error was raised.
- If get_field returned a ManyToManyField, the check raised admin.E109.
- If get_field raised FieldDoesNotExist, the code would then try getattr and if that also failed would raise admin.E108.
After the change, some of those flows were short-circuited by the early hasattr check, causing incorrect admin.E108 errors in cases where get_field would have succeeded or where getattr raises only when invoked on the class object.

Correct behaviour summary
The correct behavior is:
- If the list_display entry is callable or is an attribute of the ModelAdmin, accept it.
- Otherwise, attempt to retrieve the field using the model meta API (model._meta.get_field(item)). If that succeeds and the field is a ManyToManyField, report admin.E109. If it succeeds and is not a ManyToManyField, accept it.
- If get_field raises FieldDoesNotExist, then attempt getattr(model, item). If getattr raises AttributeError, report admin.E108 with the message:
  "The value of '%s' refers to '%s', which is not a callable, an attribute of '%s', or an attribute or method on '%s.%s'."
- Do not treat a None value returned by a descriptor as equivalent to an AttributeError; handle actual exceptions via the exception-handling logic described above.

Proposed fix (described)
The patch I propose implements the above behavior. The key changes are:
- Remove the early hasattr(model, item) check so that a False from hasattr does not prevent trying model._meta.get_field(item). A False hasattr can be caused by a descriptor on the field object that raises when accessed on the class rather than indicating the field truly does not exist.
- Use exception handling around get_field and getattr to distinguish between the different failure modes.
- Only return admin.E108 if both attempts to obtain the attribute (via model._meta.get_field and getattr) fail.
- If a field is obtained and it is a ManyToManyField, return admin.E109.
- The None return from a descriptor is not used as a signal of AttributeError; instead the correct behavior is determined by whether exceptions were raised.

This approach preserves the fix for the original ticket 28490 while avoiding the regression that causes admin.E108 to be raised for fields that are only accessible via instances (such as PositionField).

problem_statement:
Title: Calling the order_by method on a parent model crashes when Meta.ordering contains expressions

Description

(last modified by Jonny Fuller)

Hi friends,

During testing I discovered a strange bug when using a query expression for ordering with multi-table inheritance. You can find the full write up and a reproducible test repository at https://github.com/JonnyWaffles/djangoordermetabug. The bug occurs because the ordering field is an OrderBy object rather than a string when the get_order_dir function runs. The stack trace linked in the repository should make the issue obvious, but what I don't understand is why it only fails during test database setup and not when used in an interactive REPL or a standalone script. I wish I could help more and come up with a real solution. Hopefully this is enough for someone wiser to find the culprit.

problem_statement:
Add DISTINCT support for average and sum aggregates.

Description

As an extension of issue 28658, aggregate functions should support the DISTINCT option for other general aggregates such as the average and sum functions. Before version 2.2, these aggregations simply ignored the DISTINCT parameter, but now they throw an exception.

This change would involve marking the relevant classes as allowing the DISTINCT option, and the same approach could be applied to the minimum and maximum aggregates as well (although that would be largely unnecessary).

problem_statement:
simplify_regexp doesn't replace trailing groups.
Description

The function replace_named_groups fails to replace the final named group if the urlpattern passed in is missing a trailing '/'. For example, with input that represents a regular expression matching a URL like entries/<pk>/relationships/<related_field> — where the pk named group matches any characters except a slash or a dot, and the related_field named group matches word characters — the related_field group does not get properly replaced. A workaround is to add a '/' at the end of the pattern, after which it works.

Code that reproduces this is attached.
This function is used downstream in Django REST Framework. See issue 6888

OuterRef in exclude() or ~Q() uses wrong model.
Description

The following test (added to tests/queries/test_qs_combinators) fails when trying to exclude results using OuterRef.

The test exercises three cases:

- filter(): A Number queryset is annotated with a boolean field named foo defined by an Exists subquery over Item, where the subquery filters Item by tags__category_id equal to an OuterRef referencing the Number's pk. Hi! I am new in the django community, so please help me, because I really don't know if this is a "bug".

I have a Django project named "testproject" and two apps: testapp1 and testapp2.

To illustrate:

- In testapp1 there is a model named App1. It defines an "id" field that is a UUIDField used as the primary key, marked unique, with a default UUID generator, not editable, and a verbose name "identifier". It also has a "text" field (a short text field with a maximum length of 100 and verbose name "text") and a field named "another_app" that was originally a UUIDField allowing null and blank values and with verbose name "another app".

- In testapp2 there is a model named App2. It defines an "id" field that is a UUIDField used as the primary key, marked unique, with a default UUID generator, not editable, and a verbose name "identifier". It also has a "text" field similar to the one above.

After some time I changed the "another_app" field in App1 from a UUIDField to a ForeignKey pointing to App2, allowing null and blank values, using SET_NULL as the on-delete behavior, and keeping the same verbose name.

When I created a new migration after that change, the Migration class did not include any dependency for App2 even though the field is now a ForeignKey. I expected the migration to create a dependency on testapp2.App2 because of the foreign key relationship.

This project uses Django version 2.2 and PostgreSQL. I attached an archive with the sources. The project contains a small test; after running it you get the following exception:

ValueError: Related model 'testapp2.App2' cannot be resolved.

So is this a problem in Django or am I misunderstanding something?

Here is my post in django-users:
https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/django-users/Django$20bug$3A$20change$20uuid$20field$20to$20FK$20does$20not$20create$20dependency%7Csort:date/django-users/-h9LZxFomLU/yz-NLi1cDgAJ

Regards, Viktor Lomakin

Adjusting dependencies allows the test to pass: dependencies = [ ('testapp1', '0002_app1_another_app'), ('testapp2', '0001_initial'), ] Thus, AlterField should pick this up. (Note for later: SQLite will require disabling constraint checking for this, ref #30023.)
That's probably a bug in django.db.migrations.autodetector.MigrationAutodetector.generate_altered_fields's ​call to add_operation which doesn't pass any dependencies when new_field.is_relation and not old_field.is_relation. The dependencies can be retrieved by using self._get_dependencies_for_foreign_key(new_field). We want to depend on the latest migration of the referenced app instead of the initial one though as the model we're referencing might have been altered since then but that's something the aforementioned method should handle. problem_statement:
call_command fails when an argument of a required mutually exclusive group is passed in kwargs.

Description

Error message:
django.core.management.base.CommandError: Error: one of the arguments --shop-id --shop is required

This error is raised when I invoke the management command using call_command while passing shop_id as a keyword argument (shop_id=1). The shop_id argument is part of a required mutually exclusive group created on the parser: the group is required and contains two options, one named --shop-id that accepts an optional integer and is stored as shop_id, and one named --shop that accepts an optional string and is stored as shop_name.

However, invoking the command by passing the option string --shop-id=1 to call_command works fine.

In the Django source I found that only those keyword arguments passed into call_command that correspond to parser actions which are individually marked as required are forwarded to the parser. In other words, the implementation only builds parse arguments from actions that have their required flag set and whose destination is present in the provided options. In this special case neither of the two mutually exclusive options is individually required; they are only required as part of their mutually exclusive group. The call_command implementation does not consider groups defined on the parser, so it fails to pass the provided shop_id keyword through to satisfy the group's requirement.

problem_statement:
Migrations uses value of enum object instead of its name.
Description

(last modified by oasl)

When using an Enum object as the default value for a CharField, the generated migration file uses the Enum member's value instead of its name. This causes a problem when using Django translation on the Enum value.

The problem is that, when the Enum value gets translated to the user's language, the old migration files raise an error stating that the Enum does not have the corresponding value (because the Enum value has been translated to another language).

Example:
Suppose models.py defines an Enum called Status with members GOOD and BAD whose values are created via Django's lazy translation of the strings "Good" and "Bad". The Enum's string representation returns the member name. A model Item has a status field defined as a CharField with default set to the Status.GOOD member and max_length set to 128.

In the generated migration file, the status field default is represented by constructing the Enum from its value "Good" rather than by referencing the Enum member by name; the field still has max_length 128.

After translation, the word "Good" will be translated to another word and will no longer match any value in the Status Enum, so the migration raises this error:
ValueError: 'Good' is not a valid Status

Shouldn't the code generated by the migration use the name of the Status Enum member (for example, the name GOOD) rather than the value, since the value is changeable by translation? The migration should reference the Enum member by its name (accessing the member named GOOD), which will remain correct regardless of translations of the visible value.

problem_statement:
models.E015 is raised when a model's ordering configuration includes the primary-key lookup of a related field.

Description

The models.E015 validation error is triggered when the model's Meta ordering setting includes a lookup that targets the primary key of a related object. For example, specifying ordering that refers to the primary key of a related "option" field on a model in test_app.SomeModel results in an error stating: 'ordering' refers to the nonexistent field, related field, or lookup 'option__pk'. This behavior is a regression introduced in commit 440505cb2cadbe1a5b9fba246bcde6c04f51d07e.

django.utils.http.parse_http_date two digit year check is incorrect

Description

(last modified by Ad Timmering)

RFC 850 does not mention this, but in RFC 7231 (and there's something similar in RFC 2822), there's the following quote:
Recipients of a timestamp value in rfc850-date format, which uses a two-digit year, MUST interpret a timestamp that appears to be more than 50 years in the future as representing the most recent year in the past that had the same last two digits.

Current logic is hard coded to consider years with the last two digits 0–69 as belonging to 2000–2069, and 70–99 as belonging to 1970–1999, instead of comparing the two-digit year against the current year to decide whether it should be interpreted as a recent past year per the RFC guidance.

problem_statement:
Form Field’s __deepcopy__ does not (deep)copy the error messages.
Description

The deepcopy method defined for the form fields in the fields module performs a shallow copy of the field instance and does not perform additional handling for the error_messages dictionary. As a result, all copies of the same field share the same error_messages dictionary and any modification of that dictionary or of an error message value for one form field is immediately reflected on all other form fields.

This affects Forms and ModelForms that modify their fields' error messages dynamically: while each instance of a particular form (for example, a profile form) is expected to have its own independent set of fields, in practice all instances share the same error messages, which leads to incorrectly raised errors.

Confirmed for versions of Django going back to 1.11.

problem_statement:
Combine fast delete queries
Description

When emulating ON DELETE CASCADE via on_delete=models.CASCADE the deletion.Collector will try to perform fast queries which are delete operations that match primary keys using an IN clause. There are a few conditions required for this fast path to be taken, but when it happens the collection logic should combine such queries by table to reduce the number of roundtrips to the database.

For example, given the following models: a Person model that has a self-referential many-to-many relationship named friends; a User model; and an Entry model that has two foreign keys to User named created_by and updated_by. Deleting a Person instance or deleting a User instance will result in multiple delete operations such as:
- a delete on the person_friends join table filtering where from_id equals the deleted id
- a delete on the person_friends join table filtering where to_id equals the deleted id
- a delete on the person table filtering where id equals the deleted id
- a delete on the entry table filtering where created_by_id equals the deleted id
- a delete on the entry table filtering where updated_by_id equals the deleted id
- a delete on the user table filtering where id equals the deleted id

But both deletes that target the same table (or N deletes depending on the number of foreign relationships) can be combined into a single delete by OR-ing the conditions. For example:
- a single delete on the person_friends table where from_id equals the id OR to_id equals the id
- a single delete on the entry table where created_by_id equals the id OR updated_by_id equals the id

Combining queries in this way would reduce the number of database roundtrips while preserving the same semantics.

The rewritten issue description following the required style.

Title
bulk_create batch_size param overrides the compatible batch size calculation

Description

(last modified by Ahmet Kucuk)

At this line: https://github.com/django/django/blob/stable/2.2.x/django/db/models/query.py#L1197
the batch_size parameter overrides the compatible batch size calculation. This looks like a bug as bulk_update properly picks the minimum of the two relevant sizes:
https://github.com/django/django/blob/stable/2.2.x/django/db/models/query.py#L504

I suggest using similar logic in bulk_create as well: when a batch_size is provided, set the effective batch size to the smaller of the provided batch_size and max_batch_size; if no batch_size is provided, use max_batch_size. I am happy to open a PR for it.

problem_statement:
The value of a TextChoices/IntegerChoices field has a differing type

Description

When a model has a CharField or IntegerField whose choices parameter is set to a TextChoices or IntegerChoices subclass, the value returned by the field's getter can differ in type depending on whether the instance was just created or retrieved from the database. In particular, the in-memory value can be an enum.Enum member, while the value loaded from the database is the underlying primitive (str or int).

Example model (described)
- A TextChoices subclass is defined with two members whose values are the strings "first" and "second", each with a human-readable label.
- A Django model has a CharField with max_length set and choices pointing to that TextChoices subclass.

Example test case (described)
- The test creates an object setting the CharField to the enum member corresponding to the first choice.
- The first test asserts that the created object's field is an instance of str and that its string representation equals "first".
- The second test fetches the last object from the database and asserts the same: that the field is a str and that its string representation equals "first".

Test results (described)
- Running the tests produced one failure. The assertion for the created object failed because its string representation was the enum member's representation rather than the raw value. The assertion error shows that the observed string was the enum member representation instead of "first".

Observed behavior and impact
- When invoking the field's string conversion, the returned value for a newly created, in-memory object is the enum member representation rather than the enum member's value. This leads to inconsistent behavior compared to a retrieved instance, which yields the primitive value.
- This discrepancy can cause unexpected issues, for example when serializing data to send to an external API: a freshly created instance may produce the enum member representation (e.g., MyEnum.MyValue) while a retrieved instance produces the underlying value (e.g., my_value).

Affected APIs and parameters
- TextChoices and IntegerChoices
- CharField and IntegerField with the choices parameter
- enum.Enum-derived choice members

problem_statement:
Cannot override get_FOO_display() in Django 2.2+.

Description

I cannot override the get_FIELD_display function on models since version 2.2. It works in version 2.1.

Example:
A Django model named FooBar defines a character field foo_bar with two choices: the value 1 mapped to "foo" and the value 2 mapped to "bar". The model's string representation calls the get_foo_bar_display() method, expecting it to return the human-readable choice. Additionally, the model defines its own get_foo_bar_display method that returns the literal string "something". In Django 2.2 this results in the string representation returning "foo" or "bar", whereas in Django 2.1 it returned "something".

What I expect is that I should be able to override this function.

I don't think it should be marked as blocker since it looks like it was never supported, because it depends on the order of attrs passed in ModelBase.__new__(). OK, so there is a behaviour change here, but Sergey is correct that it does depend on attr order, so it's hard to say that this can be said to ever have been thought of as supported, with the exact example provided. This example produces the opposite result on 2.1 (even on >=PY36): def test_overriding_display_backwards(self): class FooBar2(models.Model): def get_foo_bar_display(self): return "something" foo_bar = models.CharField("foo", choices=[(1, 'foo'), (2, 'bar')]) f = FooBar2(foo_bar=1) # This returns 'foo' or 'bar' in both 2.2 and 2.1 self.assertEqual(f.get_foo_bar_display(), "foo") Because get_foo_bar_display() is defined before foo_bar is gets replaced in the the add_to_class() step. Semantically order shouldn't make a difference. Given that it does, I can't see that we're bound to maintain that behaviour. (There's a possible fix in Field.contribute_to_class() but implementing that just reverses the pass/fail behaviour depending on order...) Rather, the correct way to implement this on 2.2+ is: def test_overriding_display(self): class FooBar(models.Model): foo_bar = models.CharField("foo", choices=[(1, 'foo'), (2, 'bar')]) def _get_FIELD_display(self, field): if field.attname == 'foo_bar': return "something" return super()._get_FIELD_display(field) f = FooBar(foo_bar=1) self.assertEqual(f.get_foo_bar_display(), "something") This is stable for declaration order on version 2.2+. This approach requires overriding _get_FIELD_display() before declaring fields on 2.1, because otherwise Model._get_FIELD_display() is picked up during Field.contribute_to_class(). This ordering dependency is, ultimately, the same issue that was addressed in a68ea231012434b522ce45c513d84add516afa60, and the follow-up in #30254. The behaviour in 2.1 (and before) was incorrect. Yes, there's a behaviour change here but it's a bugfix, and all bugfixes are breaking changes if you're depending on the broken behaviour. I'm going to downgrade this from Release Blocker accordingly. I'll reclassify this as a Documentation issue and provide the working example, as overriding _get_FIELD_display() is a legitimate use-case I'd guess.

Description

Changes introduced in issue number 30687 cause an input value that is a list to be converted into a tuple, which breaks exact value queries. This behavior impacts ORM field types that rely on the input type matching exactly, for example PickledField. The expected behavior is that when an iterable is provided as input, the returned iterable type should match the input iterable type (i.e., a list in should yield a list out).

Title: makemigrations produces incorrect path for inner classes

Description

When you define a subclass of Django's Field as an inner class of some other class and then use that field inside a django.db.models.Model, running manage.py makemigrations produces a migration file that refers to the inner class as if it were a top-level class in the module rather than an attribute of its outer class.

To reproduce, define an outer class that contains an inner class which inherits from Django's CharField, and then define a Django model that uses that inner class as a field. After running makemigrations, the generated migration contains the CreateModel entry for the model and an entry for the field, but the field is referenced as if the inner class were a top-level class in the module — the outer class qualification is missing.

In the real-life case this happened with an EnumField from django-enumfields. A model defines an inner Enum subclass (decorated with enum.unique) and then declares an EnumField using that inner Enum class. The resulting migration's EnumField references the enum argument as if the Enum class were defined at the top level of the module, omitting the model class qualifier (i.e., it treats the inner Enum as a module-level class rather than as ModelClass.Enum).

The core issue is that makemigrations records the path to inner classes incorrectly by omitting the outer class, resulting in imports and references in migrations that do not point to the actual nested class.

problem_statement:
docutils reports an error rendering view docstring when the first line is not empty
Description

Currently admindoc works correctly only with docstrings where the first line is empty, and all Django docstrings are formatted in this way. However usually the docstring text starts at the first line, for example a function whose triple-quoted docstring begins immediately on the first line, and this causes an error:

Error in "default-role" directive:
no content permitted.
.. default-role:: cmsreference

The culprit is code in trim_docstring that computes indentation by taking the minimum leading-space length across the entries in the lines sequence, ignoring only empty lines. The problem is that the indentation of the first line is zero, which skews the minimum.

The solution is to skip the first line when computing that minimum, i.e., consider only subsequent lines when measuring leading spaces.

Thanks.

problem_statement:
Change in behaviour when saving a model instance with an explicit pk value if the pk field has a default
Description
	 
		(last modified by Reupen Shah)
	 
Consider the following model:
A model named Sample that has a UUID primary key field called id, where the id field has its default set to uuid4, and a name field that is a character field allowing blank values and limited to 100 characters.

In Django 2.2 and earlier, the following sequence would result in an INSERT followed by an UPDATE:
- Create a Sample instance without specifying any fields.
- Create a new Sample instance with its primary key set to the same value as the first instance and set the name to "Test 1".
- Call save() on the new instance.

However, in Django 3.0, performing those same steps results in two INSERTs (naturally the second one fails). The behaviour also changes if the default of uuid4 is removed from the id field.

This seems related to https://code.djangoproject.com/ticket/29260.

The change in behaviour also has the side effect of changing the behaviour of the loaddata management command when the fixture contains explicit pk values and the objects already exist (for example, when loading the fixture multiple times).

Perhaps the intention was to only change the behaviour if an explicit pk value was not set on the model instance being saved? (At least, that would be more backwards-compatible behaviour...)

problem_statement:
Custom template tags raise TemplateSyntaxError when keyword-only arguments with defaults are provided.
Description

(last modified by P-Seebauer)

When creating simple tags without variable keyword arguments but with a keyword-only argument that has a default value, it's not possible to supply that keyword from the template. For example: a simple tag named hello is defined to accept only a keyword-only parameter named greeting with default value 'hello' and returns the greeting followed by the word "world". Calling this template tag in a template with greeting='hi' raises the error "'hello' received unexpected keyword argument 'greeting'".

Also, supplying the same keyword argument a second time in the template raises the wrong error message. For example: a simple tag named hi is defined to require a keyword-only parameter named greeting and returns the greeting followed by "world". Calling this template tag in a template with greeting='hi' and again greeting='hello' raises the error "'hi' received unexpected keyword argument 'greeting'" instead of the correct "'hi' received multiple values for keyword argument 'greeting'".

The same behavior occurs for inclusion tags because they use the same underlying code. I already have a fix ready and will push it after creating the ticket (I have a ticket number for the commit).

This affects all versions since the offending line was introduced in 2.0…

problem_statement:
Enumeration Types are not usable in templates.
Description
	 
		(last modified by Mariusz Felisiak)
	 
The new enumeration types are great but can't be used in Django templates due to their being callable. For example, a Django template that tries to test whether a student's year in school equals the enumeration member corresponding to freshman (i.e., compares the student's year_in_school to YearInSchool.FRESHMAN) fails to work. This is because the YearInSchool type, being a class, is callable, and Django Templates always call callables with no arguments. The call fails because the required value argument is missing.
The easy solution would be to declare the do_not_call_in_templates attribute on the various Choices classes and set it to True.

problem_statement:
JSON fields are not properly displayed in the admin when they are readonly.
Description

Values stored in JSONField are displayed as a Python dict when readonly in the admin. For example, a JSON object with a key "foo" and value "bar" would be displayed using Python-style single-quoted dictionary syntax rather than valid JSON, which is not valid JSON output. I believe the fix would be to add a special case in the django.contrib.admin.utils.display_for_field to call the prepare_value method of the JSON field, rather than calling the JSON serialization routine directly, so that the InvalidJSONInput case is handled correctly.

I then define a subclass called Picking that includes two OneToOne relationships to Document: one is the implicit parent link used for model inheritance (a OneToOne relationship pointing to the parent with parent_link=True and a specific related_name), and the other is a separate OneToOne relationship named origin that points to Document with a related_name of 'picking' and on_delete set to PROTECT. First issue is that order seems to matter? Even if ordering is required "by design" (It shouldn't be — we have an explicit parent_link marker) shouldn't the framework inspect fields from top to bottom like it does with managers and other things?

problem_statement:
ModelForm RadioSelect widget for foreign keys should not present a blank option if blank=False on the model

Description

Unlike the select widget, where a blank option is idiomatic even for required fields, radioselect has an inherent unfilled state that makes the "-------" option look suspiciously like a valid choice.

In the example, a model named TestRun defines a foreign key field named data_file that points to BatchData, with on_delete set to SET_NULL, null allowed (null=True), but blank not allowed (blank=False).

A ModelForm for TestRun includes only the data_file field and specifies that the data_file widget should be a RadioSelect.

When rendering that form field, the output is an unordered list of radio buttons. The first radio button is checked by default and corresponds to an empty value with the label "---------". The next radio button corresponds to a valid related object (value "1") with the label "First Data File".

Instead, there should be no checked option for RadioSelect's input elements when rendering a new form from a model if blank is not a valid selection.

problem_statement:
Add secure default for the SECURE_REFERRER_POLICY / Referrer-Policy header

Description

A previous change (issue #29406) added the ability for the SECURE_REFERRER_POLICY setting to control the Referrer-Policy HTTP header, introduced in Django 3.0. I propose changing the default for this setting to a value that only sends the Referer header for requests to the same origin, to reduce information leakage to third-party sites.

The main risk of breakage would be linked websites that depend on the Referer header for verification. Relying on the Referer header for security is fragile because it can be spoofed.

Documentation: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Referrer-Policy
The MDN support grid is out of date: https://caniuse.com/#search=Referrer-Policy

problem_statement:
Using SimpleLazyObject with a nested subquery annotation fails.
Description

(last modified by Jordan Ephron)

Prior to commit 35431298226165986ad07e91f9d3aca721ff38ec it was possible to use a SimpleLazyObject in a queryset as demonstrated below. This new behavior appears to be a regression.

Models
- There are three Django models involved:
  - A: an otherwise empty model.
  - B: has a ForeignKey to A.
  - C: has an owner field which is a ForeignKey to the User model from django.contrib.auth.models.

TestCase
- The test builds a nested Subquery to determine an owner value for A:
  - It constructs a Subquery on B where B is filtered using OuterRef referring to A's primary key. That Subquery is annotated to expose an owner_user value derived from a Subquery that selects the owner field from C (using values for the owner field) and then the outer Subquery itself is reduced to a values selection for owner_user.
  - A SimpleLazyObject is created which will lazily create a User instance when evaluated.
  - The A queryset is annotated with a Subquery based on the previously-built owner_user subquery and then filtered where that annotated owner_user is equal to the SimpleLazyObject user.
- Apologies for the somewhat arbitrary testcase; hopefully the description is sufficient to reproduce the issue.

Results
- The operation fails with a TypeError stating: "int() argument must be a string, a bytes-like object or a number, not 'SimpleLazyObject'".
- The failure happens when the field preparation logic attempts to coerce the provided value to an integer (via get_prep_value) and encounters the SimpleLazyObject instead of a concrete int-like value, causing the TypeError.
hints_text:
I agree that this behavior was changed in 35431298226165986ad07e91f9d3aca721ff38ec, but you can easily create a test with SimpleLazyObject() (which is not a public API) and Subquery() that always fails with TypeError, e.g. def test_subquery_filter_by_lazy(self): test_user = SimpleLazyObject(lambda: get_user_model().objects.get(username='test')) qs = Company.objects.annotate( related=Subquery(Employee.objects.filter(lastname=OuterRef('ceo__lastname')).values('user')), ).filter(related=test_user) self.assertEqual(qs.get(), self.foobar_ltd) This is somehow related with nested subqueries.
Alright so here's what's happening here. When the most outer filter(owner_user=user) call is made the lookup logic tries to resolve owner_user's output_field in order to get_lookup('exact') on it. owner_user points to Subquery(owner_user) and it's .output_field is self.query.output_field. Since .values('owner_user') refers to Subquery(C.objects.values('owner')) which refers to self.query.output_field which refers to a column mapping to a Col referencing C.owner the actual outer most filter(owner_user=user) left hand side output field is whatever sql.Query.output_field returns for a selected field. problem_statement:
Migration crashes deleting an index_together if there is a unique_together on the same fields

Description

Happens with Django 1.11.10

Steps to reproduce:
1) Create models with two fields, and add the same two fields to both unique_together and index_together.
2) Delete the index_together entry -> migration fails.

The migration fails with an error: ValueError: Found wrong number (2) of constraints for ... This happens because the migration logic finds two constraints for the same columns: the unique constraint and the index constraint, and cannot resolve them.

The worst part for me was that this occurred while I was refactoring to use the new Options.indexes feature in Django 1.11. I was not trying to remove the actual index, only changing how it is declared in the code.

I think there are two separate issues here:
1) Deleting an index_together should be possible on its own, or migrations should handle index_together and unique_together coherently.
2) Moving the declaration of an index (for example, from index_together to Options.indexes) should not cause the index to be recreated unnecessarily.

problem_statement:
Simplify signature of DatabaseOperations.execute_sql_flush

Description

The current signature is a method named execute_sql_flush that takes the parameters using and sql_list.

The using argument can be dropped and inferred by the calling instance via its connection alias.

problem_statement:
FieldError when migrating field to new model subclass.
Description

Analogous to #21890. If creating a model subclass and moving a field onto it in the same step, makemigrations works but migrate dies with django.core.exceptions.FieldError: Local field 'title' in class 'Book' clashes with field of the same name from base class 'Readable'.

For example, initially there is a model named Readable that defines a field title as a character field with max_length=200. The change is to make Readable have no fields and introduce a new model named Book that subclasses Readable and defines title as a character field with max_length=200.

The migration is generated with CreateModel for Book, then RemoveField for Readable.title. But running it produces the error.

Reversing the order of the migration operations makes it pass. The auto-detector should be able to use this order.

problem_statement:
Model.objects.all().delete() subquery usage performance regression
Description

Lock tests are failing with Django-MySQL on Django 3.1: https://github.com/adamchainz/django-mysql/pull/660.

The tests run Model.objects.all().delete().

Django 3.0 generated a simple DELETE statement that removed all rows from the table testapp_alphabet.

Django 3.1 generates a DELETE statement that deletes rows from testapp_alphabet using a WHERE clause with an IN subquery that selects id from the same table.

The presence of the subquery blocks using LOCK TABLES together with delete(), as described in the MySQL documentation: you cannot refer to a locked table multiple times in a single query using the same name; you must use aliases instead and obtain a separate lock for the table and each alias. The documentation gives an example where attempting to operate on a table that was not locked for the specific name results in the error:
ERROR 1100: Table 't' was not locked with LOCK TABLES
Because the subquery refers to the same table without an alias, there is no way to lock it properly.

Additionally this change is a performance regression. I benchmarked with MariaDB 10.3 on an InnoDB table populated with 100,000 rows using the sequence storage engine. Using the old plain DELETE FROM form, deleting the 100k rows took approximately 0.2 seconds. Using the DELETE ... WHERE id IN (subquery) form, deleting the same 100k rows took approximately 7.5 seconds.

Yes, in theory the optimizer could recognize and optimize this, and it may be fixed in later MySQL/MariaDB versions. But I think we shouldn't change the SQL here.

problem_statement:
Title
Constant expressions of an ExpressionWrapper object are incorrectly placed at the GROUP BY clause

Description

I have a function that expects an arbitrary query expression and constructs a query on a Postgres database.

The function wraps the provided expression using ExpressionWrapper with an IntegerField output, annotates that wrapped expression as expr_res on the model, then applies values over expr_res and column_a and finally annotates a sum aggregation over column_b. When the provided expression is a constant expression such as the value 3, Django generates an SQL query that includes that constant expression in the GROUP BY clause. In other words, the SQL selects column_a, the constant 3 as expr_res, and SUM(column_b), and ends up grouping by both column_a and the constant 3.

This leads to an exception because in Postgres the resulting query is invalid. The error raised is:
django.db.utils.ProgrammingError: aggregate functions are not allowed in GROUP BY

Note that when the provided query expression is not wrapped by ExpressionWrapper, Django correctly identifies the expression as a constant and omits the constant from the GROUP BY clause. For example, if the function directly annotates expr_res as the constant value 3 with an IntegerField output and then applies values and the sum annotation, the generated SQL selects column_a, 3 as expr_res, and SUM(column_b) and the GROUP BY only includes column_a, which runs correctly.

Can you confirm the following patch against master resolves your issue? diff --git a/django/db/models/expressions.py b/django/db/models/expressions.py index c1a76584f0..6bd1471692 100644 --- a/django/db/models/expressions.py +++ b/django/db/models/expressions.py @@ -863,6 +863,9 @@ class ExpressionWrapper(Expression): def get_source_expressions(self): return [self.expression] + def get_group_by_cols(self, alias=None): + return self.expression.get_group_by_cols(alias=alias) + def as_sql(self, compiler, connection): return self.expression.as_sql(compiler, connection) The underlying issue is that BaseExpression.get_group_by_cols which ExpressionWrapper inherits defaults to returning [self] when it doesn't contain aggregates while Value.get_group_by_cols is overridden to return []. Deferring grouping column resolution to the wrapped expression makes more sense IMO.
Indeed, the patch above resolves the issue!
Would you be interested in submitting a PR with the above patch and a regression test in tests/expression/tests.py? A SimpleTestCase subclass with a test method that creates a ExpressionWrapper(Value(42)) and asserts the return value of get_group_by_cols(alias=None) is [] should do!

problem_statement:
Queryset raises NotSupportedError when RHS has filterable=False attribute.
Description
	 
		(last modified by Nicolas Baccelli)
	 
I'm migrating my app to Django 3.0.7 and I hit a strange behavior using a model class that includes a Boolean field named filterable. The first model is a product metadata type model that defines a label field (a unique short text label) and a Boolean field called filterable. The second model is a product metadata model that includes a primary key id, a foreign key to a product model, a value text field, a foreign key to a marketplace model, a date_created datetime with a default, and a foreign key named metadata_type pointing to the product metadata type model.

An error occurs when filtering product metadata by value and by metadata_type. I was filtering for value "Dark Vador" and metadata_type equal to my brand metadata instance. The Django query construction raised an exception: the query building calls into Django's filter-checking logic and ultimately raises NotSupportedError with the message "ProductMetaDataType is disallowed in the filter clause."

Renaming the Boolean field from filterable to filterable_test fixed the issue. This behavior should be documented or fixed.

problem_statement:
Self referencing foreign key doesn't correctly order by a relation "_id" field.

Description

Initially discovered on version 2.2.10 but verified still happens on 3.0.6. The setup uses two Django models where the first model has a class-level default ordering of "-id", an id primary key, a self-referencing foreign-key field named "root" (nullable), and a "oneval" BigInteger field. The second model has an id primary key, a foreign-key field named "record" that points to the first model, and a "twoval" BigInteger field.

A queryset that filters the second model by the related record's oneval being in [1,2,3] and then orders by the related field "record__root_id" produces unexpected SQL and results. The generated SQL performs an inner join to the related model and then an additional left outer join to the same model (an extra join), and the ORDER BY clause sorts by the joined table's id in descending order. That descending sort appears to come from the default ordering on the first model class, but I would expect an explicit order_by to take precedence. The extra join appears to be caused by the self-referencing nature of the "root" foreign key. When "root" points to a different model (not self), the problem does not occur.

Note also that ordering by "record__root" (i.e., the relation itself) produces the same SQL behavior.

A different ordering, where the queryset orders by the deeper lookup "record__root__id", produces the expected SQL: only a single inner join and an ORDER BY on the first model's root_id column in ascending order. That seems optimal.

So is this a potential bug or a misunderstanding on my part?

There is a working workaround: annotate the queryset with a computed column named "root_id" that references the related record's root_id, then order by that annotated "root_id". The resulting SQL uses a single inner join and an ascending ORDER BY on the computed column, which matches the expected behavior and is acceptable because I need that output column anyway.

One final oddity: when using the original queryset but inverting the sort to "-record__root_id", the generated SQL again includes the two joins but the ORDER BY is ascending on the joined table's id. This suggests that the explicit negative ordering is not simply inverting the class-level sort order, which I would not expect to happen; testing on simpler cases does not show class-level ordering being inverted by an order_by with a minus sign.

Thanks for any assistance and clarification.

problem_statement:
Title
ForeignKey.validate() should validate using the base manager.

Description

ForeignKey.validate() should validate using the base manager instead of the default manager.

Consider this setup:
- A custom manager named ArticleManager is defined to return only non-archived articles by filtering archived=False in its queryset.
- An Article model has a title field and an archived boolean field that defaults to False, and its default manager (objects) is set to the custom ArticleManager so archived articles are excluded by default.
- A FavoriteArticles model has a ForeignKey to Article with on_delete set to cascade.
- A ModelForm for FavoriteArticles is created that exposes all fields. In the form's initializer, the article field's queryset is explicitly set to use the model's base manager so that archived articles are included for selection.

Because the form explicitly uses the base manager to allow archived articles, one would expect selecting an archived article to validate. However, the form will never validate as True when a user selects an archived article. This happens because the ForeignKey validation uses _default_manager instead of _base_manager. The user-facing error message is:
"article instance with id 123 does not exist."
which is confusing to typical users.

The code path for this validation comes from the ForeignKey validation implementation (see the referenced file on GitHub):
https://github.com/django/django/blob/94f63b926fd32d7a7b6e2591ef72aa8f040f25cc/django/db/models/fields/related.py#L917-L919

The FavoriteArticles form is specifically designed to use a different manager, but the ForeignKey validation prevents this from working as intended. In this example scenario, changing the model's default manager is not acceptable because the default manager must continue to exclude archived articles in other contexts.

Suggested solution: ForeignKey validation should use the model's _base_manager so it does not apply the default-manager filters during validation.

problem_statement:
Title
makemigrations crashes for ForeignKey with mixed-case app name.

Description
When I run the Django migration command on Django 3.1b1 I get the following error (the same project works on Django 3.0):

ValueError: The field DJ_RegLogin.Content.category was declared with a lazy reference to 'dj_reglogin.category', but app 'dj_reglogin' isn't installed.

models.py (Conflict Part)
There is a Category model that defines a title field (a short text field indexed for lookups), a slug field (also indexed), human-readable verbose names for the model and its plural form, a string representation that returns the title, and a method that returns the URL for viewing a category using the category slug.

There is a Content model that defines a title field (short text, unique), a slug field (unique), a rich-text body field configured with the default editor configuration, a posted timestamp field that is indexed and automatically set when created, a many-to-many relationship to the Site model, an IP address field that is not editable via forms, a category field that is a foreign-key relationship to the Category model with cascade deletion, a user foreign-key to the User model with non-null, non-blank and non-editable constraints, a status field with limited choices and a default of "draft", a string representation that returns the title, and a method that returns the URL for viewing the post using the post slug.

settings.py (Related to issue part)
The installed apps list includes a custom app with a mixed-case name (DJ_RegLogin), the usual Django contrib apps for admin, authentication, content types, sessions, messages and static files, and additional apps such as social authentication, a rich-text editor, and site-related contrib apps like sites, flatpages and sitemaps.

apps.py
The app configuration declares a custom AppConfig subclass that sets the application name to the mixed-case identifier DJ_RegLogin and provides a verbose name of "Contents".

Summary
The error indicates that Django is trying to resolve a lazy reference to a lowercased app label (dj_reglogin) for the Content.category foreign key, but that app label is not recognized as installed. The project uses a mixed-case package/app name (DJ_RegLogin) and an AppConfig that names the app using the same mixed-case identifier; this mismatch appears to trigger the migration-time failure in Django 3.1b1.

Description

When evaluating that queryset (for example, converting it to a list), an error occurs during conversion of the duration value. The operation raises the following error:

decimal.InvalidOperation: [<class 'decimal.ConversionSyntax'>]

This issue happens on SQLite and MySQL when using duration-only expressions in annotations.

problem_statement:
QuerySet.none() on combined queries returns all results.
Description

I came across this issue on Stack Overflow. I'm not 100% sure it's a bug, but it does seem strange. The example setup is as follows:

- There is a Publication model (no special fields in the example).
- There is an Article model that has a many-to-many relationship to Publication.
- There is an ArticleForm that declares a ModelMultipleChoiceField for the publications field. In one version the queryset for that field is built by combining two filtered querysets with the OR operator: one filter selects publications with id less than 2 and the other selects publications with id greater than 5. The ArticleAdmin uses this form.

That version works as expected. However, changing the ModelMultipleChoiceField queryset to use the union() method to combine the two filtered querysets breaks things. In this alternative version, the form correctly displays only the matching objects, but if you submit the form without selecting any publications (an empty submission), ALL objects matching the combined queryset are added to the article. Using the OR-combined queryset results in NO objects being added on an empty submission, which is the expected behavior.

Affected APIs / concepts mentioned: ModelMultipleChoiceField, queryset construction via filter with parameters id__lt and id__gt, combining querysets using the OR operator versus using union(), many-to-many relationship handling in forms and ModelAdmin.
hints_text: Thanks for the report. QuerySet.none() doesn't work properly on combined querysets, it returns all results instead of an empty queryset.

problem_statement:
HttpResponse.delete_cookie() should preserve cookie's samesite.

Description

We noticed we were getting this warning message from Firefox:
'Cookie “messages” will be soon rejected because it has the “sameSite” attribute set to “none” or an invalid value, without the “secure” attribute. To know more about the “sameSite“ attribute, read ​https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Set-Cookie/SameSite'

We are getting this from the messages system but it doesn't look like an issue with the messages app. The Set-Cookie header for the messages cookie on the POST includes HttpOnly, Path=/, and SameSite=Lax. The POST returns a 304 and the subsequent GET returns a Set-Cookie header that expires the messages cookie immediately (empty value, expires set to the epoch, Max-Age=0, Path=/). It looks like the code is expiring the cookie so the browser will delete it.

As we dug into what might be causing this we noticed that messages is using the response's delete_cookie method to expire the cookie if there is no message data. HttpResponseBase's delete_cookie method doesn't seem to set the SameSite attribute on Set-Cookie headers. It also only sets the Secure flag if the cookie's key begins with the prefixes __Secure- or __Host-. Chrome and Firefox will soon begin ignoring Set-Cookie headers with SameSite=None that aren't marked Secure. This could result in Chrome and Firefox ignoring all cookies deleted through HttpResponseBase's delete_cookie method if the cookie key does not start with __Secure- or __Host-.

For testing I modified delete_cookie to call set_cookie with arguments that force the cookie to expire and carry through the cookie-related settings. Concretely, the change made delete_cookie call set_cookie with max_age set to 0 and an explicit expires date to expire the cookie, path set from the path parameter, domain set to the provided domain or falling back to the session cookie domain setting, secure set when the session secure setting is enabled or when the cookie key starts with __Secure- or __Host-, httponly set from the session httponly setting (or None), and samesite set from the session samesite setting.

Definitely wouldn't want to use the session cookie settings for everything, but changing this stopped the warnings from coming in on Firefox. I copied the keyword arguments from the messages code.

Thought this might be worth a report.

problem_statement:
Make validators include the provided value in ValidationError

Description

It is sometimes desirable to include the provided value in a custom error message. For example, instead of a generic message you want an error that explicitly mentions the invalid input value, such as a message that says the provided value is not a valid email.

By making built-in validators provide the value to ValidationError, one can override an error message and use a %(value)s placeholder. This placeholder usage matches an example already in the docs:
https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/3.0/ref/validators/#writing-validators
hints_text:
​https://github.com/django/django/pull/13212
After reconsideration I have some doubts. Do you think it's really useful to include invalid values in error messages? Invalid form is redisplayed with errors in most (all?) of cases, so I'm not sure if it can be useful to display error messages containing invalid values next to form fields with invalid values (see comment). I'm trying to find a use case.
Invalid form is redisplayed with errors in most (all?) of cases This assumes the form system is used only for a narrow set of use cases that involving HTML rendering. This is not always the case, especially in projects I work on. The form system has two major features: input validation and HTML rendering. I often use the validation system without the HTML rendering. When used in this context, yes, being able to include the provided value in custom error messages is quite helpful. Sometimes this error is displayed in a log other times as an alert. I opened this ticket as my application has practical uses for it, not theoretical. I hit a wall when trying to change an error message to meet an internal specification. As a concrete example, my application allows uploading spreadsheets and the data in those spreadsheets is validated using a Django form. This use case has a history of support: see #24229. In the event of invalid data, the precise error can't be displayed next to the originating value. Providing the submitted value as context in the message helps the user locate and correct it. For example Email “blah” in cell A1 is not a valid email address. Beyond my concrete use case, the code change is quite minimal (IMO) and unobtrusive while providing more flexibility and control for users to customize error messages. I think we should give users that power as it comes with a low maintenance cost.
Sounds reasonable, thanks.

problem_statement:
TemplateView.get_context_data()'s kwargs returns SimpleLazyObjects that causes a crash when filtering.
Description

Example that worked in Django 3.0 but not in 3.1:
- A class-based template view defines a get_context_data method. The method retrieves an offer_slug from the keyword arguments using kwargs.get with a default empty string, looks up an Account object filtered by slug using get_object_or_404, and returns a context containing the found offer and the offer_slug.

In Django 3.1 you must explicitly convert the result of kwargs.get() to a string to force resolution of the lazy value:
- The same view will work if the value obtained from kwargs.get is explicitly converted to a string before passing it to get_object_or_404 so that the SimpleLazyObject is resolved.

The error generated if you don't is:
- Error binding parameter 0 - probably unsupported type

The URL configuration in both cases uses a slug converter that captures an offer_slug parameter and routes to the view.

When debugging, I found that the value coming from kwargs.get was of type 'SimpleLazyObject' in Django 3.1, and explicitly converting it to a string made get_object_or_404 behave as expected.

Environment: Python 3.7.8 with SQLite.

Passing URL kwargs into context is deprecated (see #19878) but should still work in Django 3.1 and 3.2. Regression in 4ed534758cb6a11df9f49baddecca5a6cdda9311.  def apply_limit_choices_to_to_formfield(formfield):
     """Apply limit_choices_to to the formfield's queryset if needed."""
+    from django.db.models import Exists, OuterRef, Q
     if hasattr(formfield, 'queryset') and hasattr(formfield, 'get_limit_choices_to'):
         limit_choices_to = formfield.get_limit_choices_to()
-        if limit_choices_to is not None:

problem_statement:
limit_choices_to on a ForeignKey can render duplicate options in formfield

Description

problem_statement:
FileField with a callable storage does not deconstruct properly

Description

A FileField with a callable storage parameter should not evaluate the callable when it is being deconstructed.

The project documentation explains that you can pass a callable as the storage parameter for the model file and image fields. The intent is to allow the storage backend to be selected or modified at runtime, for example to use different storages in different environments.

However, the current behavior evaluates that callable during deconstruction. This breaks the runtime-varying storage assumption: when the field is deconstructed (which happens during the makemigrations operation), the actual evaluated Storage object is inlined into the deconstructed field instead of preserving the original callable reference.

The correct behavior is to return a reference to the original callable during deconstruction. For comparison, a file field that uses a callable for its upload_to parameter already behaves correctly: the deconstructed value is a reference to the callable.

This bug was introduced in the initial implementation that allowed the storage parameter to be callable: https://github.com/django/django/pull/8477, which addressed ticket https://code.djangoproject.com/ticket/28184

problem_statement:
Coroutine passed to the first middleware's process_response() instead of HttpResponse.
Description

Like the title says, using ASGI (uvicorn in my case), the first middleware (according to the list in settings.py) receives a coroutine as its response parameter, while all other middlewares down the line receive a django.http.response.HttpResponse object.

This seems to have caused an issue in the django-cors-headers package which is often placed first in order:
https://github.com/adamchainz/django-cors-headers/issues/558

How to reproduce:
- Set up a Django 3.1 project with an async server (uvicorn).
- Create a dummy class-based middleware that overrides the process_response method and prints the types/classes of the request and response parameters it receives.
- Configure the middleware as the first entry in the MIDDLEWARE setting, with other middlewares (for example the security middleware) following it.
- Launch the server and perform any request. Observe console output showing that the request is an instance of django.core.handlers.asgi.ASGIRequest and the response is a coroutine.
- Move the middleware further down the MIDDLEWARE list, restart the server and perform a request again. Observe console output showing that the response is a django.http.response.HttpResponse object.

Tentatively accepted for investigation. It's not about the first middleware because if you have only one it gets HttpResponse, but if you have at least two then then the first in a chain gets coroutine. Andrew, Can you take a look?
I think it's a bug in SecurityMiddleware : its __init__ does not call super().__init__(). This causes MiddlewareMixin._async_check() to not be called during init and the _is_coroutine magic attribute to be missing despite the async_capable=True declaration.
Hi Kevin. That's a good spot! :) Would you fancy taking on a quick PR for this? (It's on my list if not but...) Thanks
Hi ! Yeah I can do a PR for that :) I see that the cache-related middlewares have the same issue, would you prefer a common PR with all middlewares fixed or should I make a separate PR for the cache ? The 3 cache middlewares (UpdateCacheMiddleware, FetchFromCacheMiddleware, CacheMiddleware) will probably need to be changed together since they are related by inheritance.
Hi Kevin. would you prefer a common PR with all middlewares fixed or should I make a separate PR for the cache ? It’s a single issue no, a single PR, should be fine. (We can maybe do three commits if that seems better, but it’s a single issue no? :) I didn’t dig in yet, so you’re ahead of me but, if you can narrow down the issue in a test case (or three...) then that’s the main thing I’d think. Thanks for the input! Super. 👌

problem_statement:
Add support for tzinfo parameter to TruncDate() and TruncTime().

Description

(last modified by Joe Jackson)

Description
TruncDate inherits from TruncBase, which includes the TimeZone mixin. This should allow a developer to pass in a tzinfo object to be used when converting TruncDate, but the implementation actually uses the return value from get_current_timezone_name() unconditionally and completely discards the passed-in tzinfo object. The result is that attempting to aggregate by date doesn't work for timezones other than the global django.utils.timezone. For example, I can't have the django app be in UTC and pass the "America/New_York" timezone in.

Here's the offending line: https://github.com/django/django/blob/master/django/db/models/functions/datetime.py#L295

Note that a similar issue is happening in TruncTime.

Here's the method I would expect it to use: https://github.com/django/django/blob/master/django/db/models/functions/datetime.py#L17

Example
A model named TimeSlots has a DateTimeField called start_at. A timezone variable is created using pytz.timezone for "America/New_York". A query attempts to annotate a field start_date by truncating start_at to a date using TruncDate with the tzinfo parameter set to that timezone, then groups/aggregates by that annotated start_date and counts timeslots. I would expect this to group by date in the specified timezone, but currently the results are wrong for any timezone other than the one returned by django.utils.timezone.

Workaround
There was a workaround for me. I was able to use TruncDay and then convert the DateTimes returned outside of the database, but I found no way to convert from DateTime to Date in the database. Maybe a Cast would work, but I would expect TruncDate to work.

problem_statement:
Abstract model field should not be equal across models
Description

Consider an abstract base model named A that defines a field called myfield of integer type, and two concrete subclasses named B and C that inherit from A. If I collect the field objects for B and C into a shared set, one of the fields gets de-duplicated because the two field objects compare as equal. I found this surprising; in practice using a list was sufficient for my need. The root of the issue is that field equality currently only considers the creation_counter attribute.

Concretely: putting B's myfield and C's myfield into a set yields a set with a single element, and direct equality comparison of B's myfield and C's myfield returns True.

We should adjust the Field equality method so that if the field.model is different, the fields compare unequal. Similarly, it is probably wise to adjust the Field hashing method and the ordering method to match the new equality semantics.

When adjusting ordering, it may be wise to order first by creation_counter so that cases not affected by this equality collision won't be re-ordered. In an experimental branch, one test broke when ordering by model first.

I raised this on the django-dev IRC channel to check my intuitions, and others there agreed that the current behavior is not intuitive.

problem_statement:
Queryset with values()/values_list() crashes when recreated from a pickled query.

Description

I am pickling query objects (the queryset.query attribute) for later re-evaluation as per the Django documentation on pickling querysets. However, when I rerun a query that combines values and annotate to implement a GROUP BY, the result is broken.

Normally, the result of the query is a list of dictionaries, but in this case instances of the model are returned. Their internal state is broken and it is impossible to even access the id attribute because an AttributeError occurs: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'attname'.

Minimum reproducible example (described)

- Model definition: a Toy model with three fields — name (CharField, max length 16), material (CharField, max length 16), and price (PositiveIntegerField).

- Setup steps: three Toy instances are created with the following values:
  - name "foo", price 10, material "wood"
  - name "bar", price 20, material "plastic"
  - name "baz", price 100, material "wood"

- Original query: a queryset is built that groups by the material field and annotates the total price per material (using Sum over price). Evaluating this original queryset yields the expected list of dictionaries; the first element is a dictionary as expected.

- Recreated query: I take the query object from the original grouped queryset, pickle and unpickle it, and assign the unpickled query to the query attribute of a fresh queryset (for example, a queryset obtained from all Toys). After this replacement, evaluating the recreated queryset shows that the first element is an instance of the Toy model instead of a dictionary. Attempting to print or otherwise evaluate this queryset leads to an AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'attname'.

From my point of view it seems as though Django retrieves the correct aggregated data from the database, but instead of returning them as dictionaries it tries to construct model instances from them, which fails because the data structure does not match what model instantiation expects.
hints_text:
It seems that I have found the culprit. The queryset has an attribute _iterable_class, which in case of a .objects.all() type of query is ModelIterable, but when .values() is used, it should be ValuesIterable. Unfortunately, this is an attribute of the queryset, not of the query and thus it does not get pickled and unpickled. If I add prices2._iterable_class = ValuesIterable after settings prices2.query, the result is OK and everything works as expected. From my point of view, the solution would be to either add the information about _iterable_class into the pickled query object or at least update the documentation and inform users they should deal with it themselves. However, as it is a private attribute, the latter is not a very nice solution.
