Bug in posix implementation of django/core/files/locks.py
Description

The posix version of locks (the version which supports import fcntl) has a bug. The code attempts to return True to indicate success or failure acquiring a lock, but instead it always returns False. The reason is that cpython fcntl module returns None if successful, and raises an OSError to indicate failure (see https://docs.python.org/3/library/fcntl.html#fcntl.flock).
Anyone interested in using the non-blocking (i.e. locks.LOCKS_NB) requires a valid return value to know if they have successfully acquired the lock.

I believe the correct implementation should be the following:

- In the posix branch, the lock function (named lock with parameters f, flags) should call the fcntl flock operation on the file descriptor and treat a successful call (which in CPython returns None) as success, returning True. If fcntl.flock raises an OSError, the function should catch that exception and return False.

- Similarly, the unlock function (named unlock with parameter f) should call the fcntl flock operation with the unlock flag (LOCK_UN) on the file descriptor and return True on success. If fcntl.flock raises an OSError when trying to unlock, the function should catch it and return False.

This change ensures correct boolean return values for both lock and unlock, so callers using non-blocking locks.LOCKS_NB can determine whether they successfully acquired the lock.

problem_statement:
Title
QuerySet.ordered property is incorrect for GROUP BY queries on models with Meta.ordering.

Description

Using the annotate function on a queryset doesn't respect the default ordering set in the model's Meta class when determining whether the queryset is actually ordered. I expect a property to indicate whether the queryset will produce an ORDER BY clause, so I relied on the queryset's ordered property for this. However, that property remains truthy even when the resulting SQL will not contain an ORDER BY clause.

Example:

- First scenario: Retrieving all objects from the Foo model via the model manager produces a SQL SELECT that includes the uuid and name columns and an ORDER BY clause on the name column in ascending order. In this case the queryset's ordered property evaluates to True and the query.default_ordering attribute is also True.

- Second scenario: Applying an annotation that adds a count aggregation on the primary key and then retrieving the results produces a SQL SELECT that includes the uuid, name, and the aggregate count, and uses GROUP BY on the uuid column. Notably, this SQL does not include an ORDER BY clause. Despite that, the queryset's ordered property still evaluates to True and query.default_ordering remains True.

Additional info: I am using PostgreSQL.

problem_statement:
Title: Lag() with DecimalField crashes on SQLite.

Description

Environment: Django 3.0.7 with a SQLite database.

Model
The model used has three fields:
- modified: a DateField
- data: a FloatField
- amount: a DecimalField configured with decimal_places = 4 and max_digits = 7

Query
A query was constructed that annotates each row with a window expression. The window expression uses the Lag function to get the value of the amount field from 7 rows back, partitioned by the modified field and ordered ascending by the modified field.

Observed error
Executing the query raises an OperationalError with the message: near "OVER": syntax error. This occurs when evaluating the QuerySet.

Root cause hypothesis
The generated SQL attempts to cast the lagged decimal value to a numeric type but places the CAST around the LAG function only, with the OVER clause following the CAST. In other words, the CAST ends immediately after the LAG call rather than encompassing the entire window expression up to the final alias. This SQL arrangement causes SQLite to produce the syntax error.

Scope
This issue only happens when the lagged field is a DecimalField (the amount field). Using the same windowed Lag on the FloatField (the data field) works correctly.

Workaround
Specifying the Lag expression's output field as a floating-point type avoids the problem; in other words, forcing the Lag to treat its result as a float prevents the CAST placement issue and the error.

Summary
When annotating with a windowed Lag over a DecimalField, Django generates SQL that casts only the inner LAG call instead of the full window expression, causing SQLite to raise an OperationalError: near "OVER": syntax error. The issue does not occur for float fields, and forcing the Lag output to a float is a viable workaround.

problem_statement:
Title: debug error view doesn't respect exc.__suppress_context__ (PEP 415)

Description

Consider a view that, inside a try block, raises a RuntimeError with the message "my error", catches that exception, and then raises a new ValueError with the message "my new error" using the "raise ... from None" pattern to suppress the original context. Even though the raise uses "from None", unlike the standard Python traceback, the Django debug error view still shows the original RuntimeError.

Root cause

The problem is in the function named explicit_or_implicit_cause inside the get_traceback_frames implementation in django.views.debug (see link). That function obtains the explicit cause from the exception's __cause__ attribute and the implicit cause from the exception's __context__ attribute, and then returns whichever is present. It does not consider the exception's __suppress_context__ attribute introduced by PEP 415 (Python 3.3), so an explicit suppression of context (as performed by "raise ... from None") is ignored and the original context is still displayed in the debug view.

Expected behavior

The function should respect the exception's __suppress_context__ attribute: return the explicit cause if present; otherwise, if __suppress_context__ is true, do not return the implicit context; if __suppress_context__ is false, return the implicit context. This will match the intended semantics of "raise ... from None" and the behavior of standard Python tracebacks.

Reference

https://github.com/django/django/blob/38a21f2d9ed4f556af934498ec6a242f6a20418a/django/views/debug.py#L392

problem_statement:
Changing user's email could invalidate password reset tokens
Description
	
Sequence:
- Have account with email address foo@…
- Password reset request for that email (unused)
- foo@… account changes their email address
- Password reset email is used

The password reset email's token should be rejected at that point, but in fact it is allowed.

A fix would be to include the user's email address in the value used to generate the password reset token's hash.

Nothing forces a user to even have an email; the base user model does not require an email address. Perhaps the token-generation logic could be moved onto the user model, similar to how a session authentication hash is obtained via a model method.

problem_statement:
Skip auth.E003 system check for USERNAME_FIELD with total UniqueConstraints.
Description

Defining a user model like the following: a model subclassing the standard base user class that defines a username field as a character field with a maximum length of 30, sets USERNAME_FIELD to the username field name, and declares a model-level UniqueConstraint that enforces uniqueness on the username field (with a constraint name such as user_username_unq).

This will trigger the system check:
auth.User: (auth.E003) 'User.username' must be unique because it is named as the 'USERNAME_FIELD'.

Sometimes it’s not preferable to set the field as unique via the unique=True option because that will create an extra implicit pattern-matching index for character and text fields on PostgreSQL. The system check should be extended to verify the presence of the USERNAME_FIELD in Model._meta.constraints so that a model-level UniqueConstraint is considered sufficient. Not really sure if this classifies as a bug.

problem_statement:
Title
Random ordering unexpectedly breaks queryset aggregation

Description

Steps to reproduce:
- Define two models: Thing and Related, where Related has a foreign key to Thing.
- Create one Thing instance and two Related instances linked to that Thing.

Observed queries and results:
- Annotating Thing with the count of related objects, ordering by that count, and selecting the id and the annotated count returns a single row for the Thing with the count equal to 2, as expected.
- Annotating Thing with the count of related objects, ordering by the related field itself, and selecting id and the annotated count returns two rows for the same Thing, each with the annotated count equal to 1. This is expected in the sense that ordering by the related field breaks the grouping.
- Annotating Thing with the count of related objects, ordering randomly, and selecting id and the annotated count also returns two rows for the same Thing, each with the annotated count equal to 1. This is unexpected because ordering randomly should not affect aggregation/grouping.

Investigations:
- Dumping the generated SQL shows that the GROUP BY clause includes the random function, so the random ordering is being added to the GROUP BY and thereby breaking the aggregation.
- I traced this to django.db.models.sql.compiler.get_group_by. The compiler adds non-aggregate, non-reference order_by expressions into the group_by list, which causes the random ordering expression to be treated like a grouping expression.

Attempted fix:
- I adjusted the logic so that, when processing order_by expressions in the group_by construction, expressions that contain aggregates are skipped, expressions that are treated as references (is_ref) are skipped, and source expressions are added except when the source expression is an instance of the Random ordering expression type. In other words, Random ordering expressions are excluded from being added to group_by.
- With this change I saw the expected behavior locally and no tests failed against SQLite3 with default settings.

Notes
- The issue appears to be that non-referential, non-aggregate order_by expressions get folded into GROUP BY; Random-based ordering should not be added to GROUP BY.
- Relevant parts of the compiler API and flags referenced: django.db.models.sql.compiler.get_group_by, the contains_aggregate property on expressions, and the is_ref flag. The Random ordering expression type is the one that should be excluded from grouping.

problem_statement:
Upgrading 2.2>3.0 causes named tuples used as arguments to the range lookup to error.
Description

I noticed this while upgrading a project from 2.2 to 3.0.
This project passes named two-element tuples as arguments to range queryset filters. This works fine on 2.2. On 3.0 it causes the following error: TypeError: __new__() missing 1 required positional argument: 'far'.
This happens because the django.db.models.sql.query.Query.resolve_lookup_value implementation walks into the tuple elements to resolve lookups and then attempts to reconstitute the tuple with the resolved elements.
When it attempts to construct the new tuple it preserves the tuple type (the named tuple) but supplies an iterator to that type's constructor.
Named tuples do not have the constructor path for consuming an iterator in this way, so the constructor errors due to missing arguments.
The fix is to expand the iterator into separate constructor arguments when reconstructing the tuple so the named tuple receives its individual elements.

problem_statement:
Title
dateformat 'y' doesn't support years < 1000

Description

(last modified by Sam)

When using Django's date formatting on a date before year 999 (and similarly for years 99 and 9) with the format character "y", no leading zero is printed. This behavior is inconsistent with how the Python datetime module and PHP handle the "y" format in format strings:

- Django (version 3.1): Formatting a datetime representing the year 123 with the 'y' format outputs only the single digit '3' (missing the expected leading digit).
- Python (version 3.8): Using the two-digit year format on the same date produces '23'.
- PHP (version 7.4): Using the two-digit year format on the same date produces '23'.

I have a pull request ready for this: https://github.com/django/django/pull/13614

problem_statement:
Set disabled prop on ReadOnlyPasswordHashField
Description

Currently the django.contrib.auth.forms.UserChangeForm defines a method named clean_password that returns the initial password value to prevent (accidental) changes to the password value. It is also documented that custom forms for the User model need to define this method: https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/3.1/topics/auth/customizing/#a-full-example

A while ago the forms.Field base class gained a parameter named disabled. This parameter disables a form field by adding the HTML disabled attribute so that it won’t be editable by users. Even if a user tampers with the field’s value submitted to the server, that tampered value will be ignored in favor of the value from the form’s initial data.

It seems to me that this property could be set to True by default on the ReadOnlyPasswordHashField used to display the password hash. If so, the clean_password method would no longer be necessary and the potential pitfall of using the ReadOnlyPasswordHashField without implementing clean_password would be removed.

problem_statement:
squashmigrations does not unset model options when optimizing CreateModel and AlterModelOptions
Description

When an operation resembling an AlterModelOptions call with the parameter name set to "test_model" and the parameter options set to an empty mapping is squashed into the corresponding CreateModel operation, model options are not cleared on the resulting new CreateModel operation object.

CreateModel.reduce() updates the CreateModel's options by merging the existing options with the options from the AlterModelOptions operation (a dictionary-style merge) in the referenced source file and line (django/db/migrations/operations/models.py line 144 on commit 991dce4f). This merge approach has no logic to remove options that are not present in the operation's options, whereas AlterModelOptions.state_forwards() contains logic to remove such options.

problem_statement:
loaddata crashes on SQLite when table names are SQL keywords.
Description

Steps to reproduce:
- Create a model named Order (the name "order" is a SQL reserved word).
- Create fixtures for that model.
- Invoke the project's loaddata management command to load the fixture.

Notice that it fails with the following error. This is because the table name order is not quoted properly. The database log shows that the SQLite foreign key check is executed with the bare table name, and the operation raises the following error text:
sqlite3.OperationalError: near "order": syntax error

Root Cause
File: python3.7/site-packages/django/db/backends/sqlite3/base.py line 327
Function: check_constraints
Details: due to missing quoting around the table-name placeholder in the SQL statement that invokes SQLite's foreign-key-check operation.

In the check_constraints function, if no specific table names are provided it invokes the SQLite foreign-key-check operation without arguments. Otherwise it iterates over the provided table names and executes the SQLite foreign-key-check operation once per table name, passing the table name directly into the statement without proper quoting, and collects any reported violations. Later it iterates over the reported violations and, for each one, executes the SQLite operation that lists foreign keys for the affected table, again inserting the table name directly into that statement without proper quoting, and then indexes into the returned list to identify the specific foreign key.

Issue confirmed in
3.1.0
3.1.2

problem_statement:
MiddlewareNotUsed leaves undesired side effects when loading middleware in ASGI context

Description

I experienced strange issues when working with ASGI, the django-debug-toolbar, and my own small middleware. It was a hard problem to debug; I uploaded an example project here: https://github.com/hbielenia/asgi-djangotoolbar-bug (the repository name is misleading — I initially thought the problem was with the django-debug-toolbar).

I intentionally misconfigured the session file path setting to force a 500 error. When I start the application and access the admin URL (or any location — I kept the example minimal and did not add extra views) I get the error message: TypeError: object HttpResponse can't be used in 'await' expression. Disabling my custom dummy middleware in the example project fixes the issue and I instead receive a 500 ImproperlyConfigured response. I am not entirely sure what role the django-debug-toolbar plays here — removing the toolbar causes Daphne to return a 500 error page without debug information and no traceback appears in the console. I left the toolbar in place because it helped me approximate the cause of the issue.

I noticed in the framework's request handler code that when the middleware indicates it is unused and the processing loop skips further handling, it still overwrites the request handler variable with the result of a method that adapts the middleware to sync/async mode. On the next iteration, this adapted handler is passed to the next middleware instance, which ignores the previous checks for the presence or absence of async support. This likely causes the middleware chain to be effectively "poisoned" from that point onward, resulting in the last middleware in the response cycle returning an HttpResponse as a synchronous middleware would, instead of returning a coroutine as expected in an async context.

This issue is probably avoided if I make my middleware support async, but the documentation led me to expect that middleware intended only for synchronous requests would work as-is. My middleware is intentionally synchronous-only, so I did not make it async-compatible. If Django requires every middleware to support async when the application is run as an ASGI app, the documentation should state that explicitly. Otherwise this requirement seems to contradict the purpose of having an async_capable flag set to False in the middleware.

problem_statement:
Permit migrations in non-namespace packages that don't have the __file__ attribute
Description

Summary
This feature request, for which I will post a PR shortly, aims to improve the specificity of the migration loader's check for and rejection of PEP-420 namespace packages. I am NOT asking to allow namespace packages for apps' migrations. I merely want to make the existing check more compliant with Python's documented import API. This would remove one impediment to using Django in so-called frozen Python environments (such as those mentioned in #30950) that do not set the __file__ attribute on regular packages by default.

This narrow proposal does not change Django's behavior at all for normal Python environments. The only change for frozen environments is that Django will learn how to find existing migrations. In particular, at this time I am not proposing to enable any other Django feature that does not already work in frozen environments.

I would love for this feature to land in Django 3.2.

Details
I initially broached this idea on the django-developers mailing list. This is my second ticket related to frozen Python environments, the first being #32177.

The current implementation of the migration loader's no-namespace-package check in django.db.migrations.loader.MigrationLoader.load_disk skips searching for migrations in a module if the module's file attribute is missing or falsey.

The trouble with this implementation is that namespace packages are not the only modules with no __file__ attribute. Indeed, the Python documentation states that the file attribute is optional and that the import system may opt to leave it unset if it has no semantic meaning (for example, a module loaded from a database).

However, Python's documentation also states that namespace packages do not use an ordinary list for their path attribute; they instead use a custom iterable type. The class used for namespace packages' path in CPython is an implementation detail, but the important distinction is the type of the path attribute rather than merely the presence or absence of a file attribute.

Instead of relying solely on whether the module has a file attribute, I propose to augment the loader's check by adding an additional verification that the module's path attribute is a plain list. In other words, continue to treat modules without a normal list-type path as namespace packages, but do not reject modules merely because their file attribute is missing.

problem_statement:
Drop support for SQLite versions older than 3.9.0
Description

(last modified by Tim Graham)

Indexes on expressions (see issue 26167) and the compile-time option that enables the JSON1 extension are supported on SQLite 3.9.0 and later.

Ubuntu Xenial ships with SQLite 3.11.0 (which will still be supported by Django) and will reach end-of-life in April 2021. Debian Jessie ships with SQLite 3.8.7 and reached end-of-life on June 30, 2020.

SQLite 3.9.0 was released in October 2015. SQLite version support appears similar to the GEOS libraries situation, for which we generally continue support for about five years after release.

problem_statement:
Allow autoreloading when running Python with -m on a package other than Django
Description
	 
		(last modified by William Schwartz)
	 
The Django autoreload routine that builds child process arguments (the autoreload function in django.utils.autoreload) currently detects only when Python was launched with the -m flag specifying the Django package. It also relies on the presence of a module file attribute in modules, which is not set in all Python environments. Like issue #32177, this ticket aims to remove an impediment to creating Django-based command-line utilities that implement their own __main__ sub-module while overriding Django's built-in management commands—in this case, the runserver command.

The fix proposed in the attached pull request is to use Python's documented way of determining if the interpreter was started with -m inside the autoreload child-argument detection function. The idea follows Python's documentation about the program entry point: the module executed as the program entry point always has a spec object, and that spec object is not None exactly when Python was launched with the -m option or when a directory, zipfile, or other sys.path entry was used as the script name. In the directory-or-zipfile case, the script name is added to sys.path and the __main__.py within that location is executed as the program entry point. The spec object for that entry contains a parent attribute that corresponds to the package name and is the empty string when Python was started with the name of a directory or zip file.

Therefore, Python was started with the -m option for a given package exactly when the parent attribute of the program entry point's spec equals that package's name. Following this documented algorithm avoids depending on module file attributes and is consistent with Python's own behavior.

problem_statement:
ModelChoiceField does not provide value of invalid choice when raising ValidationError
Description
	 
		(last modified by Aaron Wiegel)
	 
Compared with ChoiceField and others, ModelChoiceField does not show the value of the invalid choice when raising a validation error. Passing in parameters with the invalid value and modifying the default error message for the code invalid_choice should fix this.
From source code:
- The ModelMultipleChoiceField is a multiple-choice field whose choices come from a model QuerySet. It sets specific widgets for normal and hidden inputs. Its default error messages include:
  - invalid_list: "Enter a list of values."
  - invalid_choice: "Select a valid choice. %(value)s is not one of the available choices."
  - invalid_pk_value: "“%(pk)s” is not a valid value."
- The ModelChoiceField is a choice field whose choices come from a model QuerySet. Although it subclasses ChoiceField, it does not actually use ChoiceField's implementation. Its default error messages include:
  - invalid_choice: "Select a valid choice. That choice is not one of the available choices."

problem_statement:
Saving parent object after setting on child leads to data loss for parents with non-numeric primary key.
Description
	 
		(last modified by Charlie DeTar)
	 
Given a model setup where there is a foreign key relation from an Order model to a Product model, and the Product model uses a non-auto CharField named sku as its primary key (with a specified maximum length), and the Order model has a product foreign-key field with on_delete set to CASCADE.

If the relation is initialized on the parent with an empty Product instance that does not yet have its primary key defined, and the primary key is subsequently set, the parent does not observe the change to the primary key:

- In a single transaction (using the transaction.atomic context manager), an Order instance is created, its product attribute is set to a newly created Product instance with no sku value at the time of assignment, the sku on that Product instance is then set to "foo", the Product is saved, and then the Order is saved.
- After these operations, a query filtering orders by product_id equal to the empty string returns a match (which is unexpected), while a query that attempts to find the order by comparing to the product instance itself does not find a match.
- Instead of product_id being populated with the product.sku value ("foo"), it is set to the empty string. The foreign key constraint that would enforce the existence of a product with sku equal to the empty string is deferred until the transaction commits. The transaction correctly fails on commit with a ForeignKeyViolation due to the non-existence of a product with an empty-string primary key.

By contrast, if the related unsaved Product instance is created with its primary key already specified before it is assigned to the Order, the values persist correctly:

- In a single transaction, an Order instance is created and its product attribute is set to a newly created Product instance that already has sku set to "foo" at initialization. The Product is saved, then the Order is saved.
- After these operations, a query for orders matching that product instance succeeds, and committing the transaction also succeeds.

This behavior suggests an issue around how the Order.product_id field is handled at assignment time, possibly related to differences in how auto-generated versus non-auto primary keys are fetched from the related instance.

problem_statement:
Title: Combining a Q object with an Exists expression using the & operator raises a TypeError

Description

Using an Exists expression on the left and a Q object on the right with the bitwise-and operator works, but reversing the order raises a TypeError.

Minimal example (described):
- Combining an Exists expression constructed over Product.objects.all with an empty Q object, using Exists on the left and Q on the right with the & operator, returns a Q object that includes the Exists expression.
- Combining an empty Q object on the left with the same Exists expression on the right, using the & operator, raises a TypeError. The error message is: TypeError: <django.db.models.expressions.Exists object at 0x7fc18dd21400>

The & (and |) operators should be commutative on Q-Exists pairs, but they are not in this case. I suspect there's a missing definition of __rand__ somewhere.

problem_statement:
MultiValueField ignores a required value of a sub field
Description
	 
		(last modified by Takayuki Hirai)
	 
A field and a form definition:

- A subclass of MultiValueField is created using MultiWidget.
- In the constructor, two subfields are defined: the first is a character field marked as not required, and the second is a character field marked as required.
- The widget for the multi-field is constructed from the widgets of the subfields.
- The parent MultiValueField is initialized with those fields and widget, with require_all_fields set to False and the multi-field itself marked as not required.
- The compress method of the multi-field returns an empty list.
- A Form is defined that includes this multi-field under the name "mf".

Observed behavior:
- When the form is submitted with empty values for both subfields (i.e. both "mf_0" and "mf_1" are empty strings), the form's is_valid method returns True. The expectation is that is_valid should return False because one of the subfields is marked as required.
- Conversely, when one subfield has a non-empty value and the other is empty (for example "mf_0" is a non-empty string and "mf_1" is an empty string), the form's is_valid method returns False.

Concrete examples described in plain terms:
- Submitting the form with both subfields empty yields a validation result of True, although it is expected to be False.
- Submitting the form with the first subfield non-empty and the second subfield empty yields a validation result of False.

If the above behavior is not expected, please fix this problem.

problem_statement:
HashedFilesMixin's post_process() yields multiple times for the same file
Description
	
As part of fixing issue #24452, the implementation of the HashedFilesMixin used by both the ManifestStaticFilesStorage and CachedStaticFilesStorage storage classes was changed so that post-processing performs several passes over the discovered static files. This multiple-pass approach is intended to ensure nested references between files are correctly handled.

Performing multiple passes is necessary and acceptable, but currently post_process() reports the same original filename multiple times back to collectstatic's collect method. For example, when running the collectstatic command with the admin app enabled, the output shows a copying message for the original admin CSS file followed by several "post-processed" messages indicating the same original file was post-processed multiple times into different hashed filenames. I would have expected only a single "post-processed" message per original file.

The problem with this behavior is:
1) collectstatic's collect method assumes the number of yields equals the number of distinct files that were post-processed. By yielding the same original file multiple times, the summary statistics shown at the end (e.g., "X files copied, ..., Y post-processed") become incorrect: there can appear to be more post-processed files than were actually copied.
2) Subclasses of ManifestStaticFilesStorage that handle yielded files as they come in end up doing duplicate work. For example, middleware or tooling that compresses files (such as Brotli compression performed by WhiteNoise) can compress the same file multiple times, increasing deploy times. S3 backends and other uploaders might likewise upload the same file multiple times.
3) Even if intermediate hashed files need to be left around temporarily, they should not be passed back to collectstatic and/or subclasses because they are an internal implementation detail. Moreover, the duplicate yields are inconsistent: not all intermediate files are yielded, and some expected intermediate instances are missing from the reported output.

Note that while this issue is related to #28604, it is different for two reasons:
1) Even if intermediate files must be retained for correctness, they should not be surfaced to collectstatic or to subclasses as if they were distinct user-facing files.
2) The duplicate yields occur even for assets that do not require changes during the second or subsequent passes. For example, another admin CSS asset produced multiple identical post-processed messages for the same original file across the multiple passes, despite no content changes requiring reprocessing.

This behavior was mentioned in the pull request that introduced the multi-pass feature: https://github.com/django/django/pull/6507#r61024158

problem_statement:
Allow calling the built-in reversed function on OrderedSet

Description

Currently, the OrderedSet class is not reversible — it cannot be passed to Python's built-in reversed function to iterate over its elements in reverse order. Supporting this would be natural because OrderedSet preserves element order. Adding support should be straightforward: implement the special reverse-iteration protocol on OrderedSet so that it can be iterated in reverse by the reversed function.

problem_statement:
Combining Q() objects with boolean expressions crashes.
Description
	 
		(last modified by jonathan-golorry)
	 
Currently Q objects with a single child are treated differently during the deconstruct process. For a Q object constructed with a single keyword lookup (for example, x=1), calling its deconstruct method returns the Q class path, an empty positional-args sequence, and a kwargs dictionary containing that lookup. For a Q object constructed with two keyword lookups (for example, x=1 and y=2), deconstruct returns the Q class path, a positional-args sequence containing the two lookup pairs, and an empty kwargs dictionary.

This causes issues when deconstructing Q objects whose sole child is not subscriptable. For example, when a Q object is constructed using an Exists expression that wraps a queryset filtered by username 'jim', calling deconstruct results in a TypeError with the message: 'Exists' object is not subscriptable. The failure occurs because deconstruct assumes the single child can be indexed into to produce kwargs.

Patch https://github.com/django/django/pull/14126 removes the special case, meaning single-child Q objects deconstruct into positional args instead of kwargs. A more backward-compatible approach would be to keep the special case and explicitly check that the child is a length-2 tuple, but it's unlikely that anyone is relying on this undocumented behavior.

 class ErroneousViewTests(SimpleTestCase):
problem_statement:
Title: ResolverMatch __repr__ does not handle functools.partial nicely

Description

(last modified by Nick Pope)

When a partial function from the functools module is passed as the view, the string representation produced by the ResolverMatch object's __repr__ method shows the func parameter simply as a functools.partial object. This is not very helpful because it does not reveal the underlying function or the arguments supplied up front by the partial. Because a functools partial object can carry pre-specified positional and keyword arguments, those need to be exposed or handled specially so they are visible in the representation. It seems straightforward to address this by unwrapping functools.partial objects in the ResolverMatch initializer so the underlying function and its pre-supplied arguments are accessible to the representation logic.

problem_statement:
Query optimization in YearLookup breaks filtering by __iso_year
Description
	 
		(last modified by Florian Demmer)
	 
The optimization to use BETWEEN instead of the EXTRACT operation in YearLookup is also registered for the __iso_year lookup, which breaks the functionality provided by ExtractIsoYear when used via the lookup. This has been broken ever since ExtractIsoYear was introduced in Django 2.2 via issue #28649 and wasn't easy to track down since ExtractIsoYear when used by itself (for example, in an annotation) works perfectly fine. The problem appears only when using the lookup in a filter, where the optimization is applied (even when an explicit annotation is present):

- When annotating a queryset with ExtractIsoYear on the start_date field and inspecting the generated SQL, the SELECT clause uses an EXTRACT('isoyear' FROM start_date) expression to produce the annotated value.

- When filtering on that annotated field for the value 2020, the generated SQL still includes the EXTRACT expression in the SELECT clause, but the WHERE clause does not reference the annotated value; instead it uses a BETWEEN range on the underlying start_date column (start_date BETWEEN 2020-01-01 AND 2020-12-31).

- When using the __iso_year lookup implicitly in a filter (for example, filtering start_date__iso_year=2020), the generated SQL likewise uses a BETWEEN range on the start_date column (start_date BETWEEN 2020-01-01 AND 2020-12-31).

This results in the wrong data being returned by filters using iso_year. This PR fixes the behaviour, reverts the invalid changes to the tests and extends one test to catch this problem: https://github.com/django/django/pull/14157

problem_statement:
DEFAULT_AUTO_FIELD subclass check fails for subclasses of BigAutoField and SmallAutoField.

Description

The project sets the DEFAULT_AUTO_FIELD setting to the dotted path example.core.models.MyBigAutoField. In the example.core.models module, the code defines a custom primary key field class that subclasses Django's BigAutoField, and it also defines a simple model class that subclasses Django's Model. When Django imports the models, it crashes with the following error message:

ValueError: Primary key 'example.core.models.MyBigAutoField' referred by DEFAULT_AUTO_FIELD must subclass AutoField.

This can be fixed in AutoFieldMeta.__subclasscheck__ by allowing subclasses of those classes in the _subclasses property.

problem_statement:
The rewritten issue description following the required style.

Title
Allow autoreloading when running Python with the -m option for a custom module and a runserver command

Description

(last modified by Mariusz Felisiak)

The original fix [1] only attempted to handle the case where the -m option was used with a two-component dotted name and the final component is a package that contains the special main module file. When a dotted module name with more than two components is specified — for example, a top-level package, a subpackage, and a module file located under that subpackage — invoking Python with the -m option and the full dotted name plus an additional command argument results in the arguments being truncated to just the first two components, which is incorrect.

[1] https://github.com/django/django/commit/ec6d2531c59466924b645f314ac33f54470d7ac3

Commit note: Fixed detection when starting non-Django modules with Python's -m option in the autoreloader.

problem_statement:
Title: database client runshell doesn't respect os.environ values in some cases

Description

(last modified by Konstantin Alekseev)

The PostgreSQL client returns an empty dictionary instead of None for the environment parameter. As a result, the process environment from os.environ is not used and an empty environment is passed to the subprocess.

This bug was introduced in the linked commit (shows the changes that caused the behavior) and is discussed in the linked pull request.

Affected concepts: os.environ, the env parameter, subprocess invocation for the database client.

Links:
- Commit that introduced the change: https://github.com/django/django/commit/bbe6fbb8768e8fb1aecb96d51c049d7ceaf802d3#diff-e98866ed4d445fbc94bb60bedffd5d8cf07af55dca6e8ffa4945931486efc3eeR23-R26
- Pull request: https://github.com/django/django/pull/14315

Title:
Q object __or__ appears to get all dunder-related default columns and queryset raises ProgrammingError.

Description

There appears to be a difference in how Q object aliases are set up when OR'ed. The get_default_columns for a filter that uses the related field id with an "in" of IDs only uses a single column, whereas get_default_columns for a filter that uses the related object queryset gets all fields. That later results in the database error "subquery must return only one column".

Example difference in behavior:
- Working case: a filter that uses the related field id with an "in" list of IDs OR a count-equals-zero condition. This uses the id list from the property_groups queryset and behaves correctly.
- Not-working case: a filter that uses the related object queryset itself with "in" OR a count-equals-zero condition. This causes all fields from the related model to be included in the subquery and triggers the error.

Error observed:
A ProgrammingError is raised with the message: "subquery must return only one column".

Workaround tried:
To force it to work, a temporary hack was added that checks the first column's alias and, if it matches the expected alias for the subquery (the U0 alias), restricts the columns list so that only the single needed field is returned. This was implemented by checking the first column alias and replacing the columns list with a single-item list when it matched the expected alias.

Regression details:
This worked on Django 2.2.5 and is now failing on Django 3.2.

How the query is built in the failing flow:
- property_groups is obtained via a manager method that returns a queryset of PropertyGroup instances for a specific management agent.
- The main queryset is annotated with a Count of the related agent__property_groups.
- The failing filter then applies an OR between: (1) checking membership of the related property_groups using the queryset returned from the manager, and (2) checking that the related property_groups count is zero. A distinct is applied on the result.

Working alternative:
Replacing the related-object membership check with a membership check against the list of IDs from the property_groups queryset (i.e., using values_list("id", flat=True) and comparing the related field id against that list) makes the query generate a correct subquery that returns only one column, and the error goes away.

What the generated SQL problem looks like (plain-language description):
The top-level SQL is a COUNT over a subselect of distinct rows. Inside that, the query groups by the main table id and the joined property group id. The problematic part is a nested subselect used in the HAVING clause that unexpectedly selects multiple columns from the related property group table (for example: id, created, updated, create_by, update_by, tenant_objs, name) rather than selecting only the id. That multi-column subselect is what causes the "subquery must return only one column" error.

Inspection of the Q object and the subquery internals:
- When inspecting the failing Q object, the related model for the subquery is the PropertyGroup model.
- The select_fields for the subquery include multiple entries corresponding to all default fields of the PropertyGroup model (multiple columns).
- The column list for the alias (U0) contains multiple columns corresponding to those fields.
- In the working case (using the id list), the select_fields contains only a single entry and the column list for the alias contains only the id column.
- The subquery object indicates it is a subquery, has aliasing enabled, and has alias mappings for U0, U1, and U2 (where U0 is the base table for PropertyGroup and U1 and U2 are join aliases). Alias reference counts show the base alias and one join alias in use.
- The table mapping shows which aliases correspond to which tables, and the where clause restricts the subquery to property groups associated with a given management agent id.

Summary and expectation:
When a Q object is used with an OR that involves a related-object queryset membership check, the ORM is including all default columns of the related model in the subquery rather than just the related key column. This leads to an invalid subquery that returns multiple columns. Using an explicit id list for the membership check results in the ORM selecting only the id in the subquery and avoids the error. The behavior changed between Django 2.2.5 and 3.2.

problem_statement:
MySQL backend uses deprecated "db" and "passwd" kwargs.
Description

The MySQL backend is passing the keyword arguments named db and passwd when establishing a connection; this behavior is visible in the referenced backend implementation file on GitHub. mysqlclient recently marked those two keyword argument names as deprecated in favor of database and password respectively. mysqlclient added support for the newer keyword names in version 1.3.8.

Django 2.2, 3.1, and 3.2 all require a minimum mysqlclient version newer than 1.3.8, so a fix that switches the backend to use database and password instead of db and passwd could be backported to all currently supported versions of Django.
hints_text: Thanks for this report. Django 2.2, 3.1, and 3.2 all require a minimum version of mysqlclient newer than 1.3.8, so a fix for this could be backported to all currently supported versions of Django. Django 2.2 and 3.1 are in extended support so they don't receive bugfixes anymore (except security patches). We'll document the maximum supported version of mysqlclient in these versions as soon as deprecated kwargs are removed. IMO we can backport this to the Django 3.2 since it's LTS.

problem_statement:
catch_all_view does not support FORCE_SCRIPT_NAME.
Description
	 
		(last modified by SlavaSkvortsov)
	 
The catch_all_view returns a redirect built from request.path_info with a trailing slash, which cuts off the configured script name (FORCE_SCRIPT_NAME). It should instead return a redirect built from request.path so that the script name is preserved.

problem_statement:
Title
ManifestStaticFilesStorage crashes with max_post_process_passes = 0.

Description

To reproduce:
- Create a subclass of ManifestStaticFilesStorage and set its max_post_process_passes attribute to 0.
- In your settings, configure STATICFILES_STORAGE to use that custom storage class.
- Run the collectstatic management command.

Resulting error
An UnboundLocalError occurs with the message: local variable 'substitutions' referenced before assignment. The failure happens during the post-processing phase of static file handling (inside the post_process implementation), where the substitutions variable is referenced even when the loop that sets it has never been entered.

Additional context
The problematic code is visible in the linked source for django/contrib/staticfiles/storage.py where substitutions is only assigned if a certain loop runs at least once: https://github.com/django/django/blob/a0a5e0f4c83acdfc6eab69754e245354689c7185/django/contrib/staticfiles/storage.py#L246-L257

Motivation
The reason for setting max_post_process_passes to 0 is to prevent Django from producing invalid CSS, as discussed in the referenced ticket comment: https://code.djangoproject.com/ticket/21080#comment:19

problem_statement:
BoundWidget.id_for_label ignores id set by ChoiceWidget.options
Description

The implementation of the BoundField.subwidgets method retrieves an id from the widget's attributes or from the form's auto_id, builds an attrs dictionary from that id, and then passes that attrs dictionary into the widget's subwidgets method (called with the field's html_name and value). The call to the field widget's subwidgets method returns a sequence of widget dictionaries; each widget's attributes dictionary contains an id entry with the value we expect to use when rendering the label of a CheckboxSelectMultiple.

However, the BoundWidget.id_for_label method ignores the id available in the widget's attributes. Instead of using the id provided in the widget's attributes, the method builds a new id string based on the bound widget's name and index, effectively re-implementing id generation and discarding the id passed in via attrs. This behavior is confusing and likely unintended. It has remained unnoticed because the form auto_id argument is rarely overridden; when auto_id is overridden, one would expect the BoundWidget.id_for_label method to render the id string specified by the auto_id format.

If the id_for_label method simply returned the id value found in the widget's attributes, the behavior would match expectations.

Please note that this issue only occurs when rendering the subwidgets of a CheckboxSelectMultiple widget. It is unrelated to the BoundField.id_for_label method.

problem_statement:
urlize() does not handle html escaped string and trailing punctuation correctly

Description

Example:
- Calling the urlize function on the text: Search for google.com/?q=1&lt! and see.
- Expected behavior: The URL substring (google.com/?q=1&lt) should be turned into an HTML link whose href is http://google.com/?q=1%3C and whose link text is google.com/?q=1&lt, with the trailing exclamation mark remaining outside the link.
- Actual behavior: The output incorrectly places the characters "lt" immediately after the closing link, so the link is followed by "lt!" before the remainder of the sentence. This duplicates part of the escaped entity and places it outside the anchor.

problem_statement:
Include number of rows matched in bulk_update return value

Description

Currently, the bulk_update function returns None, unlike the update function, which returns the number of rows matched.
It looks like it would be easy to add the same functionality to bulk_update since the implementation of bulk_update simply calls the update function repeatedly (see the Django query implementation in django/db/models/query.py).
I.e. the return values could simply be accumulated and returned.

For example, the number could be returned as a property of a named tuple with one property. That way, if a new value is requested in the future, it could be added by adding a new property to the named tuple.

The only things that occur to me right now are things like the number of queries made, and the batch size used for the function call. I took a look at this yesterday and due to the way bulk_update treats duplicates in objs this might not be quite so straight forward as simply summing the returned values from repeated update() calls. Duplicates split between batches will be counted twice. See https://code.djangoproject.com/ticket/32388

problem_statement:
Missing import statement in generated migration (NameError: name 'models' is not defined)
Description

I found a bug in Django's latest release: 3.2.4.
Given the following contents of models.py:
- The module imports django.db.models.
- It defines MyField as a subclass of the TextField class from django.db.models.
- It defines MyBaseModel as an abstract model subclassing the Model base class from django.db.models.
- It defines MyMixin as a plain mixin class.
- It defines MyModel which inherits from MyMixin and MyBaseModel, and declares a field named "name" that uses MyField with primary_key=True.

The makemigrations command will generate the following migration file:
- The migration imports the app's models module and django.db.migrations.
- It declares a Migration class with initial=True, no dependencies, and a single CreateModel operation for "MyModel".
- The CreateModel operation lists one field: "name", represented as an instance of the custom MyField from the app's models (with primary_key=True and serialize=False).
- The CreateModel options indicate the model is not abstract.
- The bases for the model are rendered as a tuple containing the mixin from the app's models module and models.Model (the Django base model class).

Which will then fail with the following error:
- The migration file raises a NameError when loaded: "NameError: name 'models' is not defined".
- This occurs when evaluating the bases tuple in the generated migration, because the migration references models.Model but the migration file does not import the module that defines "models".

Expected behavior: Django generates a migration file that is valid Python.

Actual behavior: Django generates a migration file that is missing an import statement.

I think this is a bug of the module django.db.migrations.writer, but I'm not sure. I will be happy to assist with debugging.
Thanks for your attention,
Jaap Joris

It looks like an issue with special casing of models.Model in TypeSerializer. problem_statement:
Add nonform CSS class for non form errors in FormSets
Description
	 
		(last modified by Ties Jan Hefting)
	 
Forms currently add a CSS class used to mark errors that are not tied to any specific field to the objects that collect and render form errors. This behavior is documented in the section on rendering form error messages. Similarly, for formset-level errors I'd expect a distinct CSS class to be added to mark errors that do not belong to any individual form within the formset. This would allow a custom error-list renderer to distinguish between field-specific errors, form-level non-field errors, and formset-level non-form errors when rendering error messages. Therefore I suggest adding this distinct CSS class for formset-level errors and documenting it for developers to use.

Title
BaseForm's field-cleaning and changed-data logic should access values via BoundField

Description

(last modified by Chris Jerdonek)

While working on a related ticket, I noticed that the base form's field-cleaning routine and the logic that determines which fields have changed do not currently access their values through the BoundField objects. It would be better for consistency, and to reduce the number of distinct code paths, if those routines obtained values via the BoundField.

One consequence of the current implementation is that the form's field-cleaning routine can return a different value from a field's initial value as accessed through the BoundField when they should be the same. This edge case is almost, but not quite, covered by the existing test that verifies behavior when a datetime field's initial value is provided by a callable and that callable-based behavior is disabled; that test can be adjusted to cover the remaining difference.

As part of this change, and consistent with accessing data through BoundField objects, the code would be simpler if the per-field logic that decides whether a field's data has changed were moved into a method on the BoundField class (for example, a "did change" method). Whether a form field's data has changed depends on both the field definition and the bound data, so it is more appropriate for that logic to live on the BoundField. With such a refactor, the overall changed-data routine could be reduced from roughly twenty lines to a compact routine that iterates the bound fields and asks each bound field whether it changed.

A similar simplification could be applied to the base form's field-cleaning routine so that it, too, delegates per-field behavior to the BoundField objects.

Title:
Missing call make_hashable on through_fields in ManyToManyRel

Description

In version 3.2 an identity property was added to all ForeignObjectRel instances to make them comparable. A hash is derived from that identity, which works because identity is a tuple. To make limit_choices_to hashable (one of the elements of that tuple), there is a call to make_hashable.

However, through_fields can be provided as a list. In that case, the make_hashable call is missing in ManyToManyRel, so the list remains unhashable.

For some reason this only fails when checking a proxy model. The reporter guesses proxy models run more checks than normal models, which is why the missing conversion only surfaces then, but that is not confirmed.

Minimal repro

- A model named Parent with a name field.
- A proxy model that subclasses Parent (Meta: proxy = True).
- A model named Child with:
  - a ForeignKey to Parent (on_delete CASCADE)
  - a many-to-many field to Parent that uses an explicit through model, with through_fields provided as a list containing the two field names "child" and "parent", and a related_name set.
- A through model (ManyToManyModel) with:
  - a ForeignKey to Parent with related_name set to '+' (no reverse relation)
  - a ForeignKey to Child with related_name set to '+'
  - a second ForeignKey to Child that allows null and has a default of None

Which will result in

When running Django's checks (for example via manage.py), hashing the relation identity fails because through_fields was left as a list and not made hashable, causing the process to raise the following error message: TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'. This happens when the framework attempts to hash the relation identity to compare ForeignObjectRel instances.

Solution

Add the missing call to make_hashable on self.through_fields in ManyToManyRel so that through_fields are converted to a hashable form when necessary.

problem_statement:
Provide a way for model formsets to disallow new object creation
Description

Model formsets don't provide a way to create an "edit only" view of objects. We see users trying to use the extra parameter set to zero to accomplish this, but that's not reliable as the extra parameter is merely meant to control the extra number of forms to display. Additional forms can still be added on the client side with JavaScript or by submitting additional POST data.
hints_text:
In 8e6a08e: Refs #26142 -- Documented that Formset's extra=0 doesn't prevent creating objects.
In 204d31c: [1.9.x] Refs #26142 -- Documented that Formset's extra=0 doesn't prevent creating objects. Backport of 8e6a08e937272f088902cdbec65a9f2e919783bf from master
Doesn't max_num already allow this? Testing on master, if you have max_num set to 0 and validate_max to True, then the formset is effectively edit-only for existing objects. From the ​documentation: max_num does not prevent existing objects from being displayed Is there a corner case of functionality that's not covered by these two settings?
Yes, I think it's that sending data that references pks that don't appear in the queryset creates new objects for that data.
Can you expand on that a little? Looking at the formset code, if the form number is less than the initial form count, it uses save_existing_object. Since validate_max prevents any forms above initial form count from being a valid formset, the only way a new object could be created is if save_existing_object could create new objects, which would be a bug in itself probably. Playing with it in Chrome, providing a blank value for the PK of one of the objects in the formset will cause an error when ​trying to use to_python on the PK value since the value is blank and an integer is expected. Even if that didn't fail, it would fail to find the object by its PK in the queryset. Providing a bogus value for the PK will also ​fail to look up in the queryset on the formset. This also occurs if you use a PK for an existing object that isn't in the queryset, which is good, otherwise you'd be able to modify objects outside the queryset which would be very bad. So, I'm not sure I see the path where new objects can be created if validate_max is set and max_num is 0. Doesn't mean it's not there, but it's not immediately obvious how that could occur.
I don't think max_num=0 allows editing existing instances. Such a formset will fail with "Please submit 0 or fewer forms." won't it? The idea I had to try to accomplish this is setting max_num=len(queryset) but I'm attaching a regression test demonstrating that an extra instance is created if the user edits the 'form-INITIAL_FORMS' form value.

problem_statement:
Refactor AutocompleteJsonView to support extra fields in autocomplete response

Description

(last modified by mrts)

Adding data attributes to items in ordinary non-autocomplete foreign key fields that use forms.widgets.Select-based widgets is relatively easy. This enables powerful and dynamic admin site customizations where fields from related models are updated immediately when users change the selected item.

However, adding new attributes to autocomplete field results currently requires extending contrib.admin.views.autocomplete.AutocompleteJsonView and fully overriding the get method of AutocompleteJsonView. For example, a ModelAdmin subclass can rewrite its URL patterns to map the autocomplete path to a custom view class that subclasses AutocompleteJsonView. That custom view then implements its own get method which processes the incoming request (extracting the search term, model admin, source field, and to_field_name), checks permissions, obtains the queryset, builds the view context, and returns a JSON response. In that JSON response the "results" entry is constructed by iterating over the context's object list and producing a dictionary for each object containing id, text, and an extra notes field taken from the object; the response also includes a pagination entry with a "more" boolean derived from the page object's has_next method. The downside is that, because the entire get method must be overridden, changes to AutocompleteJsonView.get over time cause a maintenance burden for custom implementations.

The proposed solution is simple, side-effect- and risk-free: add a result customization extension point to the get method by moving the lines that construct the results inside the JSON response into a separate method. Currently the JSON response is built inline by creating a list of result dictionaries for each object in the context's object list and a pagination entry. The suggestion is to replace the inline construction with a call into a new serialize_result method for each object, while leaving pagination unchanged. The serialize_result method would encapsulate the original object-to-dictionary conversion (producing the id and text entries using the to_field_name and object string representation), making it easy to override:

- The default serialize_result would return a mapping with id and text for the given object and target field name.
- A custom subclass would override serialize_result to call the parent implementation and then extend the returned mapping with additional fields such as a notes entry taken from the object.

This change would allow concise, maintainable customizations: instead of reimplementing the entire get method, custom views would only override serialize_result to add new attributes to each result.

What do you think, is this acceptable? I'm more than happy to provide the patch.

problem_statement:
Auto-reloader should pass -X options (for cpython implementation)

Description

Environment: Windows OS

Steps performed:
- Created a new Django project using Python's module invocation via winpty.
- Created a new Django app inside that project.
- Edited the app's apps.py as a demonstration for -X options. The apps.py defines an application configuration subclass that sets the default_auto_field to Django's BigAutoField and sets the app name to my_app. At the module level it opens the project's manage.py for reading and prints the stream encoding to demonstrate what encoding is in effect.
- Added the app to INSTALLED_APPS in the project's settings.
- Ran the development server using Python with the -X utf8 option and increased verbosity, via winpty. The output shows the following sequence:
  - The process prints a line indicating UTF-8 encoding.
  - It then prints another line indicating a different encoding (cp936).
  - It reports "Watching for file changes with StatReloader" and performs system checks as usual.
- Ran the development server again with the -X utf8 option and verbosity but with the auto-reloader disabled (--noreload). The output in this case shows only the line indicating UTF-8 encoding and then performs system checks.

Observed behavior:
- When the auto-reloader is enabled, two different encodings are printed: one indicating UTF-8 and another indicating cp936. This suggests the reloader's child process is not inheriting the -X utf8 option.
- When the auto-reloader is disabled, only UTF-8 is printed as expected.

Relevant references:
- Python sys _xoptions documentation: https://docs.python.org/3/library/sys.html#sys._xoptions
- Python open() documentation: https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#open

problem_statement:
method_decorator() should preserve wrapper assignments

Description

The function that is passed to the decorator is a partial object and does not have any of the attributes expected from a function i.e. __name__, __module__ etc.

Consider the following case:

- A logger decorator is defined. It uses a wrapper helper to preserve the original function's metadata. The wrapper invokes the original function, captures any exceptions and converts them to a string result, and finally logs a debug message that includes the original function's name, the positional and keyword arguments it was called with, and the resulting value or error text.

- A class defines a method that is decorated using method_decorator with the logger decorator applied. The method simply returns a fixed string when called. An instance of the class then invokes that method.

problem_statement:
Reverse time zone conversion in Trunc()/Extract() database functions.
Description

When using a time zone of Etc/GMT-10 (or similar) for a Trunc class tzinfo, there is a different behavior in the resulting database query as of Django 3.2. I believe this is due to a change in the return value of timezone._get_timezone_name() that is called by the TimezoneMixin.

On Django 3.1 the TimezoneMixin method get_tzname() returns +10 for an Etc/GMT-10 time zone after calling _get_timezone_name(). That value later becomes -10 in the generated SQL query as a result of how _prepare_tzname_delta() in the Postgres DatabaseOperations class formats the time zone offset — effectively applying a time zone 10 hours east from UTC. In other words, the DATE_TRUNC expression in the SQL ends up using an AT TIME ZONE offset of -10.

On Django 3.2 the TimezoneMixin method get_tzname() returns the literal zone name Etc/GMT-10 for an Etc/GMT-10 time zone after calling _get_timezone_name(). This later, incorrectly, becomes Etc/GMT+10 in the generated SQL query due to the return value of _prepare_tzname_delta() in the Postgres DatabaseOperations class — which corresponds to a time zone 10 hours west from UTC, i.e., the opposite direction from the Django 3.1 behavior. Concretely, the DATE_TRUNC expression in the SQL ends up using AT TIME ZONE with the reversed Etc/GMT sign.

Observed behavior in the interactive shell:
- Under Django 3.1, calling timezone._get_timezone_name() with a pytz timezone constructed for Etc/GMT-10 returns +10.
- Under Django 3.2, the same call returns the string Etc/GMT-10.

The above differences are the same when using Python's zoneinfo.ZoneInfo as the tzinfo provider.

problem_statement:
Wrong URL generated by get_admin_url for readonly field in custom Admin Site
Description

When a model containing a ForeignKey field is viewed (or edited) in a custom Admin Site, and that ForeignKey field is listed in readonly_fields, the url generated for the link is /admin/... instead of /custom-admin/.... This appears to be caused by a line in django.contrib.admin.helpers get_admin_url that calls the URL reversal function with the url name and the quoted primary key of the related object as arguments, but without specifying the current application context.

Other parts of the admin use the current_app keyword parameter to identify the correct current name of the Admin Site. (See django.contrib.admin.options.ModelAdmin response_add as just one example.)

I have been able to correct this specific issue by changing that URL reversal call so that it still passes the url name and the quoted primary key, but also sets the current_app parameter to the admin site's name obtained from the model_admin instance. However, I don't know if there are any side effects and I have not yet run the full suite of tests on this. Mostly looking for feedback whether I'm on the right track.

problem_statement:
ModelChoiceIteratorValue is not hashable.
Description

Recently I migrated from Django 3.0 to Django 3.1. In my code, I add custom data-* attributes to the select widget options. After the upgrade some of those options broke. Error is TypeError: unhashable type: 'ModelChoiceIteratorValue'.

Example (this one breaks):
- I override the create_option method (parameters: name, value, label, selected, index, subindex, attrs).
- The override calls the parent create_option to obtain the option context, and returns early if value is empty.
- It then checks whether the current value exists as a key in self.show_fields. Here, self.show_fields is a dictionary mapping an identifier to a list of field names (for example, mapping 1 to a list containing first_name and last_name).
- When the value is found in that dictionary, the code serializes the corresponding list of field names to JSON and assigns it to a data-fields attribute on the option's attributes.
- This flow triggers the unhashable type error.

However, working with arrays is not an issue:
- The same overridden create_option implementation, when checking whether value is present in a plain array of allowed_values (for example, an array containing 1 and 2), behaves correctly and does not raise the error.

problem_statement:
Title
Internationalisation didn't support language locale containing both script and region.

Description
The i18n_patterns function doesn't work with locales that contain both a script and a region, for example en-latn-us.

In the project settings, the default language is set to English (en-us) and the LANGUAGES setting includes three entries: en-us (English), en-latn-us (Latin English), and en-Latn-US (BCP 47 case format). The URL configuration uses Django's i18n_patterns to add a view that returns a simple text response 'U!'.

Observed behavior
- Requesting the URL for en-us returns HTTP 200 with body 'U!'.
- Requesting the URL for en-latn-us returns HTTP 404 Not Found.
- Requesting the URL for en-Latn-US returns HTTP 404 Not Found.

Steps to Reproduce
1. Create a new Django project.
2. In the project settings, set LANGUAGE_CODE to en-us and set LANGUAGES to include the three entries: en-us, en-latn-us, and en-Latn-US.
3. Add Django's locale middleware (LocaleMiddleware) to the MIDDLEWARE setting.
4. In the URL configuration, use i18n_patterns to add a root view that returns a plain text response 'U!'.
5. Run the database migrations and start the development server.
6. Visit the language-prefixed URLs for en-us, en-latn-us, and en-Latn-US.

The results
- The response of http://localhost:8000/en-us/ is HTTP 200 with content 'U!'.
- The response of http://localhost:8000/en-latn-us/ is HTTP 404 Not Found.
- The response of http://localhost:8000/en-Latn-US/ is HTTP 404 Not Found.

Expected behavior
The responses for http://localhost:8000/en-latn-us/ and http://localhost:8000/en-Latn-US/ should be HTTP 200 with the 'U!' response. The en-Latn-US tag follows the format defined in RFC 5646. Accept-Language and Content-Language headers follow RFC 5646. According to RFC 5646, a language tag (langtag) consists of a language subtag, optionally followed by a script subtag, optionally followed by a region subtag, optionally followed by variant subtags and extension/private-use subtags. The language subtag may be two or three letters (ISO 639), or four letters reserved for future use, or between five and eight letters for registered subtags. The script subtag is four letters (ISO 15924). The region subtag is either two letters (ISO 3166-1) or three digits (UN M.49).

Additional information
I have confirmed this issue is reproducible on a fresh Django project.

Environment
- Python version: 3.7.5
- Django version: 3.2.7

problem_statement:
KeyError with migration autodetector and FK field with hardcoded reference

Description

Hi,
I encountered this issue on an old Django project (probably 10 years old) with tons of models and probably a lot of questionable design decisions.

The symptom is that running the test suite in verbose mode fails during test database setup. The test runner creates the test database, synchronizes apps without migrations, creates many tables, runs deferred SQL, and then reports that there are no migrations to apply. At that point the process fails with a KeyError: 'to'. The failure originates in the migration autodetector: during change detection the autodetector calls its routine that filters out relation-agnostic fields and then attempts to remove the 'to' key from a field deconstruction, which raises KeyError: 'to'.

I finally did some digging and found that the culprit is a custom ForeignKey field that hardcodes its to argument and thus also removes it from its deconstructed kwargs. It seems that the autodetector doesn't like that.

Reproduction test (described)

- A CustomFKField subclass of the standard ForeignKey is implemented so that its initializer forces the 'to' argument to a specific hardcoded model reference (testapp.HardcodedModel). Its deconstruct method calls the parent's deconstruct, removes the 'to' key from the returned kwargs, and returns the deconstruction values.

- A test constructs two ProjectState instances named before and after. The before state contains a model named HardcodedModel with no fields. The after state contains the same HardcodedModel and an additional TestModel. The TestModel has a field named custom which uses the CustomFKField with on_delete set to CASCADE.

- The test invokes the migration autodetector (MigrationAutodetector) on the before and after project states and calls its change detection routine (the internal detect changes method). The test asserts that the autodetector reports one change for the app.

While I will happily admit that my custom field's design might be questionable, I don't think it's incorrect and I think the autodetector is at fault here.

Suggested fix

Changing the code that blindly deletes the 'to' key from the deconstructed kwargs to instead pop the 'to' key with a default (so no error is raised if 'to' is already absent) makes the test suite run again in verbose mode. This appears to be a small defensive fix that prevents KeyError when custom fields remove 'to' from deconstruction.

Affected APIs / functions / parameters mentioned

- MigrationAutodetector
- ProjectState, ModelState
- Field deconstruct behavior
- only_relation_agnostic_fields (autodetector routine)
- 'to' deconstructed kwarg
- on_delete parameter behavior (CASCADE mentioned)
- Exception: KeyError: 'to'

Description

Title
Query.change_aliases raises an AssertionError

Description
Python Version: 3.9.2
Django Version: 2.2.24, 3.2.9 (reproduced using two different versions)

Code to Reproduce (described)
- Models: There are four models. One model has a foreign key to another model with related_name "foos". A second model has two foreign keys to the first model with related_names "bars" and "other_bars", and also a foreign key to a third model with related_name "bars". The third model is empty. The fourth model has a many-to-many relation with the third model with related_name "quxes".
- Test flow: Create an instance of the fourth model. Let qs1 be the QuerySet of related objects obtained via that instance's "foos" relationship. Let qs2 be a QuerySet of the first model filtered by an OR of two conditions: that the "bars" relation's related third-model field is in the many-to-many set of the fourth model instance, OR that the "other_bars" relation's related third-model field is in that same many-to-many set.
- Observed behavior: Performing the union operation with qs2 on the left and qs1 on the right works fine. Performing the union with qs1 on the left and qs2 on the right raises an AssertionError.

Failure details
The failing case raises an AssertionError during alias-change logic. In the failing scenario, the mapping of aliases ends up such that one alias would be remapped to another alias, and that alias in turn would be remapped again (for example, an alias sequence that effectively maps T4 -> T5 and T5 -> T6), causing keys and values of the alias change map to intersect and triggering the assertion.

Investigation
I reproduced this as simply as I could and examined the cause. During an OR operation of two QuerySets, in Query.combine when building the combined query, if the RHS Query currently has sequential aliases (for example T4 and T5) and the related table names also exist in the LHS.table_map, calling Query.table_alias from Query.join results in creation of aliases that shift the numbering (for example assigning T5 for the old T4 and T6 for T5). This produces a change_map whose keys intersect with its values, which causes the AssertionError in Query.change_aliases.

Expectation / Suggested fixes
- A potential fix would be to allow the rhs alias_map to be provided to Query.join and Query.table_alias, and to ensure that when a new alias suffix is chosen it is incremented until it does not exist in rhs.alias_map. This would prevent intersections between the change_map keys and values.
- The assertion at the start of QuerySet.change_aliases is not documented with a comment. It appears to ensure that an alias will not be changed twice (for example first T4 -> T5 and then T5 -> T6) according to the order in change_map. A comment explaining this invariant, or an improved AssertionError message similar to other assertions in Query.combine, would be helpful.
- It seems that the QuerySet OR operation can produce different SQL depending on operand order (i.e., it is not commutative in terms of generated aliases), even though the result rows are the same. This non-commutativity could be explicitly documented.

Please investigate and consider the above fixes and documentation improvements.

Vishal Pandey, if you're looking for pointers on how to resolve the issue I think I have a pretty good understanding of the problem. The root cause is that both queries happen to share the same alias_prefix; the letter used generate aliases when the same table is referenced more than once in a query. We already have a method that does all of the heavy lifting to prevent these collisions that the ORM uses when subqueries are involved which is Query.bump_prefix but it's not entirely applicable here. I think the best way forward here is to change the alias_prefix of the rhs and change its alias accordingly so it doesn't conflict before proceeding with the creation of the change_map.

Ömer, My initial attempt was to use Query.bump_prefix but as you told it threw an error. The error you encountered is due to bump_prefix requiring some adjustments. The alias merging algorithm that Query.combine uses requires that both query share the same initial alias in order to work otherwise you'll get a KeyError. You'll want to find a way to have bump_prefix adjust all the aliases but the initial one so it can still be used as the merge starting point. --- Vishal, Here, I am randomly choosing an uppercase letter as the first character of alias, this returns different aliases, but a test_case is failing with this approach, with the following traceback. Choosing a random initial alias will bring more bad than good as not relying on alias_prefix will cause undeterministic failures across the board. There are reasons why the prefix is used and bumped only on conflic; it makes reasoning about possible collisions easier. In 2nd approach, I have rotated the alias_prefix in a circular manner from T(class variable alias_prefix has value T) to Z, then from A to Z, and so on, and it also works on the above-attested code but fails five other test cases. This approach doesn't account for possible collisions with subquery aliases and will eventually collide once you've wrapped up around the 26 letter of the alphabet instead of using the Cartesian product approach. --- All of the required logic for preventing alias_prefix collisions already lives in bump_prefix, it's only a matter of adjusting it in order to allow it to be used in the alias merging algorithm of combine.
