problem_statement:
Use simplified paths for deconstruct of expressions

Description

Previously the F expression deconstructed to the fully qualified path located in the ORM's expressions module. Because the F expression can also be imported from the higher-level models package, PR #14047 changed its deconstruction to use the path within that models package. This simplifies generated migration code because the expression will be referenced only via importing the models package from the Django db package and then accessing the F expression as an attribute on that models package.

As Mariusz pointed out on the PR, the same technique can be applied to other expressions, further simplifying generated migrations.

problem_statement:
MigrationRecorder does not obey db_router allow_migrate rules
Description
	
Hi,
We have a multi-db setup. We have one connection that is for the django project, and several connections that talk to other dbs for information (i.e. models with managed = False). Django should only create tables in the first connection, never in any of the other connections. We have a simple router whose allow_migrate method returns True when the db parameter equals 'default' and False for any other database.

Current Behaviour
We run our functional tests and the migrate command is called against each connection when the test databases are created (see django/test/runner.py, setup_databases, line 300-ish, which calls django/db/backends/creation.py, create_test_db, line 377-ish).
When this migrate runs, it tries to apply our migrations, which tries to record that a migration has been applied (see django/db/migrations/executor.py, apply_migration, which has several calls to self.recorder.record_applied). 
The first thing that record_applied does is a call to self.ensure_schema() (see django/db/migrations/recorder.py, record_applied, line 66-ish). 
ensure_schema checks to see if the Migration model is in the tables in the connection. If it does not find the table then it tries to create the table. 
I believe that this is incorrect behaviour when a db_router has been provided. If using the router above, my expectation would be that the table is not created on any connection other than the 'default' connection. Looking at the other methods on the MigrationRecorder, I would expect that there will be similar issues with applied_migrations and record_unapplied.

I wanted to chime in here to broaden the scope of the bug, as I was affected by it recently in a different context. The bigger issue is not just that the framework tries to create the migrations table where it's not needed, but that it marks as applied migrations that in fact were not. That puts the database in an inconsistent state, at least as far as migrations are concerned. It's a harmless inconsistency for the specific settings file used at that specific moment in time, but it lays the seed for big problems down the line. For example, if you later decide to change your routing scheme, or (as happened in my case) if you have multiple projects with different settings using the same app on the same database. In terms of a solution, what seems straightforward to my untrained eye is for the migration framework to simply not record migrations as applied that it didn't apply (and as a corollary, it shouldn't try to create the migration table on a database if it doesn't need to record any migrations there). The fix suggested above ("to have migrations refuse to run entirely and just exit if the migration model is not allowed to be created on the target database") doesn't address the broader issue.

Title: Optimize multiple AlterFooTogether operations into one

Description

Hi,
In issue #31503 we split the AlterFooTogether operations (the AlterUniqueTogether and AlterIndexTogether migration operations) into two kinds of operations. First, a migration will have operations that remove constraints, and then later operations that add the new constraints. This allows field alterations to work as expected during the intermediate steps.

In some cases, this produced pairs of operations that can be reduced to a single operation.

See for instance the test case at the linked pull request.

Example:
- Before optimization: there is a sequence of four migration operations on the model with parameter name set to "mymodel":
  1. An AlterUniqueTogether operation that sets unique_together to an empty set.
  2. An AlterIndexTogether operation that sets index_together to an empty set.
  3. An AlterUniqueTogether operation that sets unique_together to a set containing a single tuple with the column "col".
  4. An AlterIndexTogether operation that sets index_together to a set containing a single tuple with the column "col".

- After optimization: the sequence should be reduced to two operations on the same model:
  1. An AlterUniqueTogether operation that sets unique_together to a set containing a single tuple with the column "col".
  2. An AlterIndexTogether operation that sets index_together to a set containing a single tuple with the column "col".

This avoids performing two operations on each constraint and instead performs only the necessary single operation per constraint.

problem_statement:
Micro-optimisation for Value._resolve_output_field (by modifying CharField initializer)
Description

Currently, when annotating with a Value that contains a string, the resolution path eventually calls the Value._resolve_output_field method. The code in that path checks whether the value is a string and, if so, returns a CharField instance.

However, CharField currently assumes that its max_length attribute is always a non-null sensible value, and that requirement is enforced during system checks. As a result, creating a CharField without a max_length causes it to be given a MaxLengthValidator that cannot function correctly in this context. For example, resolving the output field for a Value wrapping the string "test" yields a CharField whose validators include a MaxLengthValidator, and attempting to validate/clean a value against that validator leads to the following error message: TypeError: '>' not supported between instances of 'int' and 'NoneType'.

Further compounding this is that MaxLengthValidator is decorated with the deconstructible decorator (both directly and indirectly via a base validator class), which has an observable cost.

Baseline measurements (current behavior) for calling the Value._resolve_output_field path on such a Value show an average time of approximately 8.1 µs, with normal variance across runs. If the deconstructible decorator is removed from the validator classes, the same measurement falls to about 6.96 µs. Ignoring the class instantiation of the validator altogether results in roughly 5.86 µs. So avoiding the unnecessary validator construction yields roughly a 2 µs improvement.

Proposed change
- Modify the CharField initializer so that it only attaches a MaxLengthValidator when max_length is not None. This mirrors the approach already taken by BinaryField for precedent.
- This change avoids instantiating a validator that will be invalid in this use-case and removes some of the performance overhead from deconstructible-decorated validators.

I have a local branch implementing this change, and all existing tests pass locally. I will push the branch to CI once I have a ticket number, so we can see if it causes any other issues and decide whether it can be accepted.

problem_statement:
Adding nullable OneToOneField crashes on SQLite.

Description

This new sqlite3 error has cropped up between building django-oauth-toolkit against Django 4.0 and the main branch for migrations.AddField of a OneToOneField (see https://github.com/jazzband/django-oauth-toolkit/issues/1064).

The operation raises the following database error:
django.db.utils.OperationalError: Cannot add a UNIQUE column

The migration attempted to alter the access token table to add a new column for the source refresh token. Concretely, the database operation tried to add a bigint column for the source refresh token ID that was NULLable, marked UNIQUE, and included a foreign-key reference to the refresh token table with a deferrable initially deferred constraint.

The relevant migration adds a field named source_refresh_token to the AccessToken model. The field is a OneToOneField configured to allow blank and null values, uses SET_NULL for on-delete behavior, points to the configured refresh token model from oauth2_settings, and uses the related name "refreshed_access_token".

I see there have been a lot of sqlite3 changes in issue/PR #33355 since the 4.0 release, so this may be related.

problem_statement:
Description

Given two models: a User model that has an email field and a kind field (a short text field with choices "ADMIN" and "REGULAR"), and a Profile model that has a full_name field and a one-to-one relationship to User.

I expected the following test scenario to pass:

- The test creates a User with email "test@example.com" and kind "ADMIN", and creates a Profile linked to that user with full_name "Test Tester".
- The test then constructs a User queryset that limits selected fields to only the email field and uses prefetching. The prefetch specifies the profile relationship, and the profile-prefetch itself prefetches the related user using a queryset that limits selected fields to only the kind field. The construction uses the prefetch APIs (prefetch_related and Prefetch) and the only selector.
- The test asserts that fetching the first user from that queryset executes three database queries.
- The test then asserts that accessing the nested attribute kind on the prefetched user (user.profile.user.kind) executes zero additional queries and equals "ADMIN".

The second assertion actually fails with the following error message:
AssertionError: 1 != 0 : 1 queries executed, 0 expected

The captured query was a query that selected the id and kind columns from the user table for the specific user id. This is exactly the query I would expect to see if kind on the inner User queryset had been deferred, which it has been according to the inner queryset.

When iterating the main queryset to fetch the user, the three queries executed appear to be correct:
- A query that selects the user id and email from the user table to return the requested user.
- A query that selects the profile id, full name, and user id from the profile table for the related user ids.
- A query that selects the user id and kind from the user table for the related user ids used during the nested prefetch.

Inspecting the nested user instance shows that its deferred fields, as reported by get_deferred_fields, include the kind field.

It appears that Django correctly determines the deferred fields when executing the inner User queryset, but the actual User instances seem to be inheriting the deferred-field set from the outer User queryset. As a result, when the kind attribute on the prefetched user is accessed, a database query is triggered.

This behavior also occurs if the relationship between Profile and User is a ForeignKey instead of a OneToOne: in that case, accessing the nested user's kind after retrieving the related object triggers a query.

I'm happy to attempt to tackle this if someone can (a) confirm whether this is actually a bug and (b) point me in the right direction for investigation. Thanks!

problem_statement:
Model Field.__hash__() should be immutable.

Description

Field.__hash__ changes value when a field is assigned to a model class.

A specific sequence reproduces the problem and results in an AssertionError: first import django.db.models, then create a CharField instance with the parameter max_length set to 200, then use that Field instance as a key in a dictionary, and finally define a Model subclass that assigns that same Field instance to one of its attributes. After these steps, checking for the original Field object in the dictionary raises an AssertionError.

The bug was introduced in #31750.

This is unlikely to have been commonly encountered because there are few use cases that put a field in a dict before it is assigned to a model class. I found a reason to do so while implementing #26472, and the behaviour was confusing.

IMO we can revert the __hash__ change from #31750. Objects with the same hash are still checked for equality, which was fixed in that ticket. But it is problematic if an object's hash changes, since that breaks its use in dictionaries.

problem_statement:
Title: bulk_update() does not work with plain F expressions

Description

Repro:

- Import the SelfRef model from the example app and retrieve the first instance.
- Assign a plain F expression that references the name field to that instance's c8 field.
- Call bulk_update for that instance, requesting an update of the c8 field; bulk_update reports one row updated.
- After refreshing the instance from the database, the c8 field contains the literal string form of the F expression instead of the value of the name column.
- Inspecting the executed SQL shows that the UPDATE statement contains the string representation of the F expression rather than resolving to the underlying column name.

The created SQL therefore contains the string repr of the F expression, instead of resolving to the column name. Looking at the source code, the culprit seems to be a too-narrow type check in the query module at the linked location: https://github.com/django/django/blob/2eed554c3fd75dae1beade79f357ffd18d3c4fdf/django/db/models/query.py#L673.

It works if the type check is changed to one of the following approaches:

- Do duck-typing: check whether the attribute has a resolve_expression attribute and, if it does not, treat it accordingly.
- Or test explicitly for expression types: check whether the attribute is an instance of Expression or of the F expression type, and, if it is not, treat it accordingly.

Title
aggregate() with 'default' after annotate() crashes.

Description

I first encountered this on a PostgreSQL project and was able to reproduce it with SQLite. Environment: Django 4.0.1, running in a Django shell on Python 3.10.2.

Behavior observed
- A typical sequence of annotating a queryset and then aggregating works as expected. For example, I confirmed the model has 95 rows, and annotating rows with their id and then aggregating the sum of the id field returned 4560.
- However, if I use the aggregate class argument default (the default parameter on aggregation classes, new in 4.0) on the aggregation after annotate, the query fails with an OperationalError: near "FROM": syntax error.
- The generated SQL was malformed: it produced a SELECT with no select list before the FROM, leading to the syntax error.

Details preserved
- Affected APIs and parameters: annotate(), aggregate(), the aggregation class Sum, and the default parameter (new in 4.0).
- Error message: OperationalError: near "FROM": syntax error.

Additional note
- Using the longer form—wrapping the aggregation in Coalesce with a fallback of 0—returns the expected numeric result (4560), so the functionality can be worked around by using Coalesce(Sum(...), 0) instead of relying on the aggregation class default.

problem_statement:
Migration autodetector crashes when renaming a model and field.
Description

The migration autodetector crashes when renaming a model and a field in a single step.

What I did
- Ran the makemigrations management command.
- When prompted to confirm renaming the model test_one.MyModel to MyModel2, I answered yes.

What happened
- The process aborted with a KeyError reporting the tuple ('test_one', 'mymodel').

Where it fails
- The failure happens inside the migration autodetector during change detection and the renamed-field generation phase. The problem appears when the autodetector attempts to look up the old model in the migration state, accessing to_state.models with the parameters app_label and old_model_name, which leads to the KeyError.

Additional info
- Reported by HoskeOwl.
- Regression introduced in commit aa4acc164d1247c0de515c959f7b09648b57dc42.

problem_statement:
filter on exists-subquery with empty queryset removes whole WHERE block
Description
	 
		(last modified by Tobias Bengfort)
	 
A queryset was constructed by filtering MyModel using a negated models.Exists subquery that was built from an empty queryset (using the none() method on MyModel's manager), combined with the name parameter set to 'test'. The resulting queryset is empty. Printing the queryset's SQL representation yields the text "EmptyResultSet".

With django-debug-toolbar the generated query is still visible, but the WHERE block is missing completely. This seems to be very similar to #33018.

Since Exists encapsulate its negation logic (see __invert__) it should catch EmptyResultSet when raised by its super() call in as_sql and return an always true predicate (e.g. 1=1). problem_statement:
ModelAdmin with defined radio_fields override empty_label
Description

ModelAdmin drops my "empty_label" and sets the default empty label. For example: I have a ModelAdmin subclass where I enable radio_fields for a field named myfield and override the formfield_for_foreignkey method. In that override, when the field name is myfield I set the empty_label entry in the kwargs to the string "I WANT TO SET MY OWN EMPTY LABEL" and then call the parent implementation. However, I never get the "I WANT TO SET MY OWN EMPTY LABEL" value in the rendered form; it is always replaced by the default empty label.

How to fix it:
In django\contrib\admin\options.py, row 234, the code currently unconditionally assigns the default translated "None" string to the empty_label entry in kwargs when the database field is blank, which overwrites any empty_label previously provided. This should be changed so that the code respects an existing empty_label value in kwargs: if an empty_label was provided, use it; otherwise, fall back to the default translated "None" when db_field.blank is True.

problem_statement:
Title
has_key, has_keys, and has_any_keys JSONField() lookups don't handle numeric keys on SQLite, MySQL, and Oracle.

Description
(last modified by TheTerrasque)

Problem
When using models.JSONField() has_key lookup with numerical keys on an SQLite database it fails to find the keys.

Versions:
- Django: 4.0.3
- Python: 3.9.6 (tags/v3.9.6:db3ff76, Jun 28 2021, 15:26:21) [MSC v.1929 64 bit (AMD64)] on win32
- sqlite3.version: 2.6.0
- sqlite3.sqlite_version: 3.35.5

Example:

Database
The database is configured to use the SQLite backend with a file named db.sqlite3.

Model
There is a model that defines a JSONField named data.

Test
A test case creates two model instances: one where the data field contains a JSON object with a string key "foo" mapping to "bar", and another where the data field contains a JSON object with a numeric-looking key "1111" mapping to "bar". Both instances are saved. The test then uses the has_key lookup on the JSONField to filter for entries with the key "foo" and separately for the key "1111", and asserts that each query returns a count of 1.

Result
The test fails when querying for the numeric-looking key. The failure message is:
AssertionError: 0 != 1 : Should have found 1 entry with key '1111'

Additional info
This has been tested on SQLite and PostgreSQL backends. The lookups work on PostgreSQL but fail on SQLite.
hints_text:
Duplicate of #30566, see comment.
Not a duplicate of #30566 This is django's models.JSONField() not postgres extension JSONField It works as expected on Postgresql, the bug is on SQLite #30566 goes directly against comments for https://code.djangoproject.com/ticket/29504 If different behavior is expected on SQLite (or postgres if majority of backend has SQLite's behavior) it should be documented
I reproduce this issue on SQLite, MySQL, and Oracle. has_key, has_keys, and has_any_keys lookups uses compile_json_path() on SQLite, MySQL, and Oracle which uses array paths for integers. We shouldn't use array paths for these lookups.

problem_statement:
Title: loaddata fails on non-default database when natural keys uses foreign keys.

Description

(last modified by François Granade)

I have a one-to-many relationship between two models, Book and Author, and both models define natural keys. Loading data from a fixture works when loading into the default database, but when I target a second database it raises an exception. I'm relatively new to natural keys and serializers, and I wouldn't expect behavior to differ between the default DB and other databases.

I've committed a test project here: https://github.com/farialima/django-bug

(Note: the problem does not appear if the data is already present in the default database.)

What I ran
I piped a JSON fixture into the Django loaddata management command, specifying the other database and JSON format. This resulted in an exception.

The reported error message
testbug.models.DoesNotExist: Author matching query does not exist.

Models (described in plain language)
- Author model:
  - Has an auto-increment primary key field named id.
  - Has a name field that is a character field and must be unique.
  - Uses a custom manager where get_by_natural_key takes a name parameter and retrieves the author by that name.
  - The natural key for an Author is the author's name.
  - The string representation combines the id and the name.

- Book model:
  - Has an auto-increment primary key field named id.
  - Has a title field.
  - Has a foreign key field author that references the Author model, with a related name of "books" and a DO_NOTHING on-delete behavior.
  - Uses a custom manager where get_by_natural_key expects a title and an author identifier; it retrieves a book by matching the title and the related author's name.
  - The natural key for a Book is composed of the book's title together with the author's natural key.
  - The natural key declares a dependency on the Author model.
  - The model enforces uniqueness on the combination of title and author.
  - The string representation shows the id, the title, and the author.

Fixture data (described)
The fixture contains two serialized objects in JSON form:
- An Author object with the name "JR Tolkien".
- A Book object with the title "The Ring" whose author is represented using the author's natural key as ["JR Tolkien"].

The fixture was generated by serializing all Author and Book objects using Django's serializers with natural foreign keys and natural primary keys enabled.

Summary
Loading this fixture into the default database works fine, but using the loaddata command to load the same fixture into a non-default database results in a DoesNotExist error stating that the referenced Author cannot be found, even though the Book's natural key references the Author by natural key.

problem_statement:
Using multiple FilteredRelation with different filters but for same relation is ignored.
Description
	 
		(last modified by lind-marcus)
	 
I have a relation that always has at least one entry with the attribute is_all=True and optionally an entry that has is_all=False but has a zone value set. I'm trying to use the FilteredRelation API together with a conditional Case/When expression so that the query will use the zone-specific related entry if it exists and fall back to the "All" entry if a zone-specific one does not exist.

What I do in the query:
- I create two filtered relation aliases using FilteredRelation on the same nested relation. The first filtered relation restricts the nested relation to rows where the nested zone equals the parent object's zone. The second filtered relation restricts the nested relation to rows where is_all is True.
- I create an alias for the price coming from the zone-specific filtered relation.
- I annotate a final price field using a Case/When expression: if the zone-specific price is null then use the price from the "All" filtered relation, otherwise use the zone-specific price.

I noticed that when I use multiple FilteredRelation instances that target the same related nested relation, the generated SQL only contains a single JOIN (inspecting the raw SQL) and the other filtered relation is effectively ignored. For example, inspecting the query SQL string shows a join corresponding to the zone-specific filtered relation but no separate join for the is_all=True filtered relation.

Is this intended behavior, or should it be possible to have multiple FilteredRelation aliases on the same relation with different conditions and have them both represented separately in the generated SQL?

problem_statement:
AlterField operation should be noop when adding/changing choices on SQLite.

Description

While writing a test case for issue #33470 I found that with SQLite, even a change that should be database-transparent—adding or changing the set of allowed choices on a field—still causes SQL to be emitted. The migration ends up creating a new table, copying data into it, dropping the old table, and renaming the new table, even though this shouldn't be needed. On PostgreSQL the same migration produces no SQL.

problem_statement:
Wrong behavior on queryset update when multiple inheritance

Description

Queryset update has a wrong behavior when a queryset's model class inherits from multiple parent models. The update is applied not to the child class instances but to instances of another parent class.

Example scenario

- There are three Django models:
  - A Base model with a primary key field named base_id and an integer field named field_base.
  - Another parent model named OtherBase with a primary key field named otherbase_id and an integer field named field_otherbase.
  - A Child model that inherits from both Base and OtherBase, with no additional fields.

- In the Django shell, two records are created on the OtherBase model with field_otherbase values 100 and 101, respectively.

- Two Child records are created with field_base and field_otherbase values set to 0 and 1 respectively.

- An update is performed on the Child queryset to set field_otherbase to 55 for all Child objects. The ORM first selects the base pointer column from the Child table, and then issues an UPDATE statement against the OtherBase table setting field_otherbase = 55 for the rows whose otherbase_id values match the primary keys discovered from the Child table. The update call returns a count of 2 rows affected.

- Inspecting the Child queryset values for field_otherbase shows the Child objects still have values 0 and 1 (unchanged).

- Inspecting OtherBase records filtered by otherbase_id values [1, 2] shows both have field_otherbase = 55.

As shown above, updating the Child queryset's field_otherbase (a field defined on the second parent) has no effect on the Child instances themselves. Worse, fields on OtherBase were modified because the query used primary keys from the Base class to identify rows in the OtherBase table.

This indicates that QuerySet.update on a multi-inherited model may target the wrong underlying table, applying changes to a parent model's table rather than to the intended child model instances.
hints_text: Thank you for your report. Confirmed this is another issue with concrete MTI. I've looked at the code and in order to address the issue both sql.UpdateQuery and sql.SQLUpdateCompiler need to be updated. The changes revolve around changing UpdateQuery.related_ids: list[int] to related_ids: dict[Model, list[int]] and making sure sql.SQLUpdateCompiler.pre_sql_setup populates query.related_ids by the parent_link of the related_updates. ​That means not only selecting the primary key of the parent model but all parent link values of child model fields being updated. From there get_related_updates can be updated to do query.add_filter("pk__in", self.related_ids[model]) instead.

Title
Unregister lookup method should clear the lookup cache.

Description

(last modified by Himanshu Balasamanta)

In the current source, the method that unregisters a lookup does not clear the lookup cache. It should clear the cache, as the complementary method that registers a lookup does clear it. Making this change also requires small updates to the schema tests, specifically the test that verifies function-based unique constraint lookups. A pull request was generated for this change: https://github.com/django/django/pull/15569

problem_statement:
Django 3.2.4+ autoreload breaks on empty string in TEMPLATES DIRS.

Description

Django versions greater than 3.2.3 change the way template directories are handled by normalizing them using pathlib.Path. Projects that set the TEMPLATES DIRS value from an environment variable or other source in a way that can produce an empty string will find that the autoreloader stops working.

For example, a common pattern that splits an environment variable into a list can produce a list that contains a single empty-string element when the environment variable is empty; the intended behavior is to filter out empty strings so the list is empty instead. Any configuration that results in DIRS containing an empty string will break autoreload.

This happens because the template_changed function in django/template/autoreload.py used to compare the empty string directly to a directory path and would never match. After normalization, the empty string is transformed into the root of the project. As a result, template_changed() will now always return True, which prevents the autoreload from triggering when application code changes.

Change that produced the regression
https://code.djangoproject.com/ticket/32744
Commits in main and stable/3.2.x:
https://github.com/django/django/commit/68357b2ca9e88c40fc00d848799813241be39129
https://github.com/django/django/commit/c0d506f5ef253f006dbff0b0092c8eecbd45eedf

problem_statement:
Errors with db_collation – no propagation to foreignkeys
Description

(last modified by typonaut)

Using a db_collation on a primary key that is also referenced by foreign keys in other models causes foreign key constraint errors in MySQL.

Model setup described in words:
- The Account model defines an id field using a short-UUID primary key form, with the column collation set to utf8_bin, an index, and a maximum length of 22.
- The Address model defines a similar short-UUID primary key and has a one-to-one relation to the Account model with cascade delete.
- The Profile model defines a similar short-UUID primary key and has an optional (nullable) foreign key to the Account model, with cascade delete.

Context and observed migration SQL (described):
- Account.id was changed from an auto-increment integer type to the short-UUID type.
- The generated migration SQL first modifies the account table id column to be a varchar(22) with collation utf8_bin. Next it modifies the account_id column in the address table to varchar(22) NOT NULL, and the account_id column in the profile table to varchar(22) NULL. Finally, it issues ADD CONSTRAINT statements to add foreign keys from address.account_id and profile.account_id to account.id.
- With that generated SQL, the ADD CONSTRAINT statements fail. This happens because the COLLATE setting (utf8_bin) is not applied to the foreign key columns (address.account_id and profile.account_id) in their MODIFY statements. The foreign key columns therefore have a different collation from the referenced primary key.

Correct behavior (described):
- The MODIFY statements for the foreign key columns must include the same collation as the primary key (utf8_bin). When the foreign key columns are explicitly modified to include the same collation, the subsequent ADD CONSTRAINT statements execute without error.

Summary:
- The collation of the primary key must match the collation of its foreign keys in MySQL; migrations that set db_collation on a primary key must also propagate that collation to referencing foreign key columns, otherwise foreign key constraint errors occur.

problem_statement:
Title: RenameIndex() crashes when unnamed index is moving backward and forward.

Description

RenameIndex should restore the old auto-generated name when an unnamed index used for unique_together is moved backward. Currently, re-applying the rename operation causes a crash. For example, in the test file tests/migrations/test_operations.py a test exercises the following scenario:

- Inside a test case for migration operations, the test opens a schema editor and, with an assertion that no database queries are issued, invokes the operation to move the index backward by calling the operation's database-backwards API with the parameters app_label, the editor, new_state, and project_state.
- The test then uses an assertion helper to confirm that an index named new_pony_test_idx exists on the target table (table_name).
- The test re-applies the renaming by opening a schema editor again and invoking the operation's database-forwards API with the parameters app_label, the editor, project_state, and new_state.
- The test again asserts that the index named new_pony_test_idx exists on the table.
- Finally, the test calls the operation's deconstruct method and asserts that the first element of the returned definition indicates the operation type RenameIndex.

On PostgreSQL this sequence fails with the following error message:
django.db.utils.ProgrammingError: relation "new_pony_test_idx" already exists

problem_statement:
Title: inspect.signature() returns incorrect signature on manager methods.

Description

(last modified by Shiva Kumar)

inspect.signature returns incorrect signature information when used on queryset methods.

Example scenario: a Django model Person is defined with a name field, and inspect.signature is invoked on the model manager method bulk_create. When inspecting the signature of Person.objects.bulk_create, the observed signature is:

actual: (*args, **kwargs)

The expected signature is:

expected: (objs, batch_size=None, ignore_conflicts=False)

IPython and Jupyter use inspect.signature internally to show documentation for objects when using the help command, and they also display the incorrect signature information for these manager/queryset methods.

Root cause
The issue is due to the implementation in the manager code at the referenced repository file and line. The code manually assigns the decorated method's name and docstring (on the lines noted), but it does not copy the complete metadata required by inspect.signature.

Proposed fix
Use functools.wraps when wrapping the original method instead of manually assigning only the __name__ and __doc__. functools.wraps copies the full set of metadata, which allows inspect.signature to return the expected signature information.

If this bug is acknowledged, please assign the ticket to me; I would like to raise a PR for this.

problem_statement:
Cannot drop unique_together constraint on a single field with its own unique=True constraint

Description

I have an erroneous unique_together constraint on a model's primary key — a unique_together constraint that specifies only the id field — that cannot be dropped by a migration. The migration appears to try to find all unique constraints on the column and expects there to be only one, but I have two — the primary key and the unique_together constraint.

Indexes:
- There is a primary key index on the id column named foo_bar_pkey.
- There is a separate unique constraint on the id column named foo_bar_id_1c3b3088c74c3b17_uniq.

Database is PostgreSQL, if that makes any difference.

On a new postgresql-based project: create a new app 'foo' with the following models.py from django.db import models class Bar(models.Model): name = models.CharField(max_length=255) class Meta: unique_together = (('id',),) ./manage.py makemigrations ./manage.py migrate comment out the 'class Meta' ./manage.py makemigrations ./manage.py migrate This is not specific to the primary key field - it happens more generally on single-field unique_together constraints that duplicate a unique=True constraint, such as: class Bar(models.Model): name = models.CharField(max_length=255, unique=True) class Meta: unique_together = (('name'),)
Can't see a good way of fixing this without breaking backwards compatibility. The alter_unique_together logic in db/backends/schema.py relies on the UNIQUE constraints generated by unique_together to be distinguishable within the database from constraints generated through other mechanisms (e.g. unique=True) - but this isn't possible when the unique_together rule only contains a single field. Another way this manifests itself is to perform the following steps, in separate migrations: create a model add unique=True to one if its fields add a unique_together constraint for that same field This results in two identical calls to _create_unique_sql, leading to a 'relation "foo_bar_name_1e64ed8ec8cfa1c7_uniq" already exists' error.

Just got hit by this bug, I believe that at least in recent versions of Django (at least 3.2.13) it is now possible to distinguish unique=True constraints from unique_together ones. At least in the application I'm working on, there seem to be two different naming schemes: For UNIQUE CONSTRAINT created with unique=True the naming scheme seems to be <table_name>_<field_name>_key For UNIQUE CONSTRAINT created with unique_together the naming scheme seems to be <table_name>_<field_names>_<hash>_uniq Note that this is extrapolated from me looking at my application's database schemas, I haven't read the code so I am unsure if this is in fact what happens all of the time. So in the case where we would want to delete a unique_together constraint that had a single field, we'd just look for foo_bar_%_uniq and drop that constraint, here is an SQL statement (in PostgreSQL) that I used in a manual migration (originally from ​https://stackoverflow.com/a/12396684) in case it can be useful to someone that comes across this bug again: DO $body$ DECLARE _con text := ( SELECT quote_ident(conname) FROM pg_constraint WHERE conrelid = 'my_table'::regclass AND contype = 'u' AND conname LIKE 'my_table_my_field_%_uniq' ); BEGIN EXECUTE 'ALTER TABLE my_table DROP CONSTRAINT ' || _con; END $body$; So I think it's possible to fix this bug now?
As a workaround, it may be possible to migrate the unique_together to a UniqueConstraint, keeping the same index name, and then dropping the UniqueConstraint. Just an idea, untested.

problem_statement:
QuerySet.only() after select_related() crash on proxy models.

Description

When I optimize a query using select_related() and only() from a proxy model I encounter an error.

Environment: Windows 10; Python 3.10; Django 4.0.5.

The query evaluation fails with a ValueError: 'id' is not in list. The error occurs during queryset evaluation when Django attempts to populate related objects for a select_related call, and ultimately raises the above ValueError.

Models:
- A base model that defines a short text field called "name".
- A proxy model that proxies the base model.
- Another model that has a foreign key to the proxy model. The foreign key uses SET_NULL on delete and allows null/blank values.

Command:
- A Django management command that, in its handle method, evaluates a queryset by listing results from the "another" model while using select_related on the foreign-key relationship named "custom" and restricting loaded fields with only using the field path "custom__name".

Investigation:
- In the Django query construction code (in django/db/models/sql/query.py around line 745) the implementation uses the current model's meta options to determine which fields to populate for related objects. If that code is adjusted to use the concrete model's meta options instead of the proxy model's meta options, the query works as expected. In other words, switching from using the proxy model's meta to using the underlying concrete model's meta avoids the ValueError and allows select_related() combined with only() to function correctly on proxy models.

Description

psql expects all options to precede the database name, if a database name is provided. For example, running the project's dbshell command while passing additional psql arguments using the -c parameter to execute a query will produce psql warnings indicating that the extra arguments were ignored. The psql output in this case includes the following lines:

psql: warning: extra command-line argument "-c" ignored
psql: warning: extra command-line argument "select * from some_table;" ignored
psql (10.21)
Type "help" for help.
some_database=>

It appears the argument list needs to be constructed in the proper order, with any options placed before the database name and the database name left at the end of the argument list.

problem_statement:
Filter floatformat drops precision in decimal numbers
Description

I discovered that the floatformat template filter may drop precision when used for Decimal numbers.

Minimal working example: After configuring the Django template engine and initializing Django, I created a template that applies the floatformat filter with precision 20 to a Decimal value "42.12345678901234567890". Rendering the template produced "42.12345678901234400000", showing the precision was lost.

I traced the bug to an incorrect conversion to Decimal within the floatformat implementation that doesn't properly support Decimal numbers. Decimal values are being converted to a machine float instead, causing the loss of precision.

A pull request has been prepared: https://github.com/django/django/pull/15863

problem_statement:
Title: Allow ModelForm meta to specify formfield_callback.

Description

(last modified by Klaas-Jan Gorter)

The function django.forms.modelform_factory returns a form class based on the class it receives as the form argument. As an additional argument it accepts a formfield_callback function. When no callback is provided the class ends up using no callback instead of inheriting the formfield_callback of the base form provided.

Example (described in plain language):
- A simple model is defined with two fields: a boolean field named "active" and a character field named "name".
- A callback function named "all_required" is defined; it obtains a form field for a model field, sets that form field's required property to True, and returns it.
- A ModelForm subclass named "MyForm" is defined that sets formfield_callback to the all_required function at the form level. Its Meta class also specifies the model and sets formfield_callback to the same all_required function, and restricts fields to "active" and "name".
- The factory function is then called to create a form class using the model and passing MyForm as the base form. The resulting class is referred to as "FactoryForm".

The expected behavior would be that FactoryForm uses the formfield_callback specified in the Meta attribute of the base form (MyForm), and therefore the fields would be required in both FactoryForm and MyForm. However, under the current behavior of modelform_factory the formfield_callback is overwritten (with the default argument of None) before the new class is constructed, and in FactoryForm the fields are not required.

I believe this is a bug, because this behavior has been observed before in Ticket #18573 in Django 1.3. The test that was proposed there was incorrect, because under the expected behavior the callback should have been called four times not two times as was asserted. (I believe this test has been removed from version 2, because I find no equivalent test in tests/model_formsets_regress.)
hints_text:
I was always the impression that formfield_callback was solely an allowed kwarg of the modelform_factory function and its friends. I believe this test has been removed from version 2, because I find no equivalent test in tests/model_formsets_regress. From what I can see the patch from #18573 was never committed and thus nothing was actually removed over the years. Given ​no tests exists for this behavior and that ​it's not documented I'll change this bug report to a feature request. That seems like a really niche use case but since I don't use Django forms much myself nowadays I'll let other folks chime in.
I agree with Simon that it's really niche and ModelForm.Meta.formfield_callback has never been a documented and ​supported feature. Nevertheless, we should support it for consistency with other Meta options (this can also simplify fix for #24974), see also a comment.

problem_statement:
Case() crashes with ~Q(pk__in=[]).

Description

The following operation generates a syntax error. It constructs a User queryset that annotates each row with an alias named _a using a Case expression. The Case uses a When condition that is the negation of a Q object checking pk__in equal to an empty list, the then branch returns True, the default branch returns False, and the output field is specified as BooleanField. The queryset is then ordered by the annotated field in descending order and reduced to only the primary key values.

The error is:
ProgrammingError: syntax error at or near "THEN"
LINE 1: ..._user"."id" FROM "users_user" ORDER BY CASE WHEN THEN true ...

The generated SQL contains an ORDER BY clause with a CASE expression that lacks a condition in the WHEN clause, effectively producing a fragment like "CASE WHEN THEN True ELSE False END", which is invalid SQL.

I expected the behavior to annotate all rows with the value True since they all match.

Relevant because the negated Q with pk__in equal to an empty list (~Q(pk__in=[])) is a sentinel value that is sometimes returned by application code.
hints_text: Thanks for the report (similar to the #33374 and #26517).

problem_statement:
Prefetch objects don't work with slices
Description

Prefetch objects do not work with sliced querysets. For example, calling prefetch_related with a Prefetch object that targets the post_set relation, supplies a queryset limited to the first three posts, and sets to_attr to example_posts produces the error: AssertionError: Cannot filter a query once a slice has been taken. This behavior is also mentioned in a StackOverflow answer. On the other hand, it does not seem to be documented in the Django documentation.

Why is it needed?

My use case seems to be a common one: I want to display a list of categories while displaying a couple of example objects from each category next to it. If I'm not mistaken there isn't currently an efficient way of doing this. Prefetching without slicing would prefetch all related objects (and there may be thousands of them) instead of just the three examples that are needed.
hints_text:
It seems to me that #26565 ("Allow Prefetch query to use .values()") is related.
Hi ludwik, #26565 is about a different issue. The only way we could support slices would be to extract it from the provided queryset to make it filterable again and apply it when in-memory joining. The prefect queryset would still have to fetch all results so I'm not sure it's worth the trouble as accessing category.example_posts[:3] would have the same effect.
Charettes, Thank you for the reply. accessing category.example_posts[:3] would have the same effect I'm pretty sure that is not correct. The end effect would obviously be the same, but the way it is achieved behind the scenes and the performance characteristics that follows would be widely different. What you propose (prefetching without limit, adding slicing in a loop after the fact) would make Django perform a database query selecting all objects from the database table and loading them into memory. This would happen when the main queryset is evaluated (that's what prefetching is all about). Then the slicing would be performed by Python in memory, on a queryset that was already evaluated. That's what I understood from ​the documentation and also how Django actually behaved in an experiment I performed couple of minutes ago. What I want to avoid is exactly this behavior - loading thousands of objects from the database to display first three of them. I would be happy with a sane workaround, but to my knowledge there isn't any.
Tentatively accepting but as you've noticed it would require a large refactor of the way prefetching is actually done. I could see Category.objects.prefetch_related(Prefetch('articles', Article.object.order_by('-published_data')[0:3], to_attr='latest_articles')) being useful but the underlying prefetch query would need to rely on subqueries, a feature the ORM is not good at for now. Maybe the addition of the ​Subquery expression could help here.
The only way to limit this Query (and to not load all the records into memory) would be to do a top-n-per-group query which I don't think the ORM is capable of. What I can suggest is: Instead of limiting the QuerySet, find a way to filter it. For example, get only the Posts in the last day, week or a month (based on the post-frequency). Category.objects.prefetch_related(Prefetch( 'post_set', queryset=Post.objects.filter( date_published__gte=datetime.date.today()-timedelta(days=7)), to_attr='example_posts', )) This way you won't load all the Posts into Memory.
If window queries are implemented (https://code.djangoproject.com/ticket/26608) then this use case could be possible in something similar to: Prefetch( 'post_set', queryset= Post.objects .annotate(_rank=Window(Rank(), partition_by='cateogry') .filter(_rank__lte=3) )
I tried the filter by rank suggestion using Django 2.0 but I get this error: django.db.utils.NotSupportedError: Window is disallowed in the filter clause.
I think there is a workaround now to in django new version as we have OuterRef and Subquery. from django.db.models import OuterRef, Subquery User.objects.all().prefetch_related('comments',queryset=Comment.objects.filter(id__in=Subquery(Comment.objects.filter(user_id=OuterRef('user_id')).values_list('id', flat=True)[:5])))
Note that the solution above might not be portable to some MySql databases, with error 1235, "This version of MySQL doesn't yet support 'LIMIT & IN/ALL/ANY/SOME subquery'"
As pointed out by others support for filter against window functions would allow prefetch_related_objects to use Rank(partition_by) to support this feature. If someone wants to give a shot at solving this particular issue before #28333 is resolved it should be doable by using a combination of Queryset.raw and Query.compile combinations.

The fonte and variavel models have a many-to-many relationship, with the field defined on the "fonte" side. The many-to-many field uses the fonte_variavel model as the "through" argument.

Models as defined across separate apps:
- In core/fonte/models.py: there is a FonteModel that defines a unique text field "nome", a text field "descricao", a required date "data_inicial", an optional date "data_final", and a many-to-many relationship named "variaveis" that points to the VariavelModel in the variavel app and declares the intermediary model by referencing the FonteVariavelModel in the fonte_variavel app. The model also sets database table and verbose name Meta options and provides a string representation returning the nome field.
- In core/variavel/models.py: there is a VariavelModel with a unique text field "nome" and a text field "descricao", plus Meta options for table and verbose names.
- In core/fonte_variavel/models.py: there is a FonteVariavelModel that contains a ForeignKey to VariavelModel with cascade delete and a ForeignKey to FonteModel with cascade delete, and Meta options including the database table name.

Generated migration for the Fonte app:
- The migration was generated by Django 4.1 and is an initial migration that depends on the first migration of the variavel app.
- The migration creates the FonteModel with an automatically created primary key field, the nome and descricao text fields, the data_inicial and optional data_final date fields, and the variaveis many-to-many field. The many-to-many field in the migration includes a through argument that references the FonteVariavelModel located in the fonte_variavel app, and the to argument that points to the VariavelModel.
- The model options in the migration reflect the same verbose names and database table name as defined in the model.

Behavior observed:
- If I place the FonteVariavelModel inside the same models file as FonteModel, the migrations run successfully.
- If I instead place FonteVariavelModel in a different app (the fonte_variavel app) while keeping the many-to-many field on FonteModel, the migration fails. Moving the VariavelModel into the Fonte app while keeping the intermediary model in a different app does not fix the failure, so the issue appears to be specific to having the ManyToMany intermediary model defined in a separate app.

Error encountered:
- While applying the Fonte initial migration, Django raised the exception: AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute '_meta'.
- In essence, during schema creation the migration code attempted to inspect the through value of the many-to-many field and expected it to be a model class object (which would have a _meta attribute), but instead encountered a string, leading to the AttributeError.

Putting everything in the same models.py file also works.

problem_statement:
__in doesn't clear selected fields on the RHS when QuerySet.alias is used after annotate

Description

A test was added to reproduce the bug; it can be placed in tests/annotations/tests.py. The test does the following in plain language:

- Build a Book queryset that filters books with pages__gt set to 400.
- Call annotate to add an annotation named book_annotate with a constant value (Value(1)).
- Call alias to add an alias named book_alias with a constant value (Value(1)).
- Build a Publisher queryset that filters using the __in lookup against the Book queryset described above (i.e., publisher objects where book__in refers to that Book queryset).
- Call values with the parameter "name" to retrieve publisher names.
- Assert that the resulting publisher names are Apress, Sams, Prentice Hall, and Morgan Kaufmann.

When running this test you should get this error:
django.db.utils.OperationalError: sub-select returns 10 columns - expected 1
hints_text:
This is a ​documented and expected behavior.
Using either .alias or .annotate works as expected without using .values to limit to 1 column. Why is that? but using both of them doesn't seem work.
Replying to Gabriel Muj: Using either .alias or .annotate works as expected without using .values to limit to 1 column. Why is that? but using both of them doesn't seem work. We have some simplification in the __in lookup that automatically limit selected fields to the pk when Query is on the right-side and the selected fields are undefined. It looks like they don't play nice when .annotate() and .alias() are mixed. Tentatively accepted for the investigation.
Whether or not the In lookups defaults a Query right-hand-side to .values('pk') is based of rhs.has_select_fields (​source) This dynamic property is based of self.select or self.annotation_select_mask so I suspect that there might be some bad logic in Query.add_annotation (​source) from the introduction of QuerySet.alias in f4ac167119e8897c398527c392ed117326496652. The self.set_annotation_mask(set(self.annotation_select).difference({alias})) ​line seems to be what causes the problem here. If annotate and alias are used then annotation_select_mask will be materialized as a mask is required to keep track of which entries in annotations must be selected and whatnot (not necessary if only using alias or annotate as the first doesn't require any selecting and the second selects all annotations) The add_annotation logic relied on to implement QuerySet.alias is not wrong per se it just happens to piggy back on the annotation masking logic that only Query.set_values relied on previously an now happens to break the heuristics in Query.has_select_fields. The proper solutions is likely to replace Query.has_select_fields by a class attribute that defaults to False and have set_values set it to True and make sure Query.clone carries the attribute over. This seems like a more durable options as that avoids trying to peek into internals to determine if a values call was performed. Gabriel, since you've already written a regression test, would you be interested in submitting a patch that takes the approach proposed above?

problem_statement:
Resolve output_field when combining numeric expressions with MOD operator.

Description

When constructing a Django query expression that computes a modulo operation, if the operand types differ (for example, Decimal and Integer), the expression's resolved result type is not set to Decimal. This differs from behavior observed with other arithmetic operators, which correctly resolve the output to Decimal when appropriate.

problem_statement:
Add transaction handling to changelist list-editable processing.

Description

It seems that the changelist view in the Django admin is not wrapped in a database transaction. Because this view can modify data in the database — specifically when using the feature that allows editing multiple items from the list view — it should be executed within a transaction to prevent the database from being left in an inconsistent state if an error occurs.
hints_text: So, this has never been wrapped in a transaction. See ​https://github.com/django/django/commit/7bc0878922 where it was added. Happy to accept as a New Feature to investigate adding that. (I can't immediately see any obvious blockers.)

problem_statement:
The check option on the makemigrations command behaves inconsistently with other commands' check options.

Description

To script a check for missing migrations but stop short of creating any migration files, you currently need to combine the check option with the dry-run option for the makemigrations command. This is inconsistent with the migrate command's check option and the optimizemigration command's check option, which simply exit (possibly after logging) without performing changes.

I propose that the makemigrations command when given the check option should also just exit without writing migration files.

The decision to create migration files anyway when check is used does not appear to have been discussed, as far as I can tell, on ticket:25604 or in the linked developer group discussion. I noticed this while reading a pull request to update the documentation for the migrate command's check option. The current documentation appears to be silent on whether the makemigrations command should write files when its check option is used.

problem_statement:
object HttpResponseNotAllowed can't be used in 'await' expression

Description

When defining a simple View subclass with only an async post method, GET requests to this view cause the following exception and a 500 response:

[29/Sep/2022 07:50:48] "GET /demo HTTP/1.1" 500 81134
Method Not Allowed (GET): /demo
Internal Server Error: /demo

The server error includes the TypeError: object HttpResponseNotAllowed can't be used in 'await' expression.

This can be easily reproduced with an empty project (no external dependencies) started with Django 4.1.1 and Python 3.10.6.

Basic view to reproduce the bug:
- Create a subclass of django.views.View named Demo that supports only POST requests.
- Implement an async post(request) method on that view which returns a django.http.HttpResponse with a simple "ok" body.

URL pattern to access it:
- Add a URL pattern that maps the path "demo" to the Demo view.

Steps to reproduce:
- Start the local development server using the standard management command for running the server.
- Open http://127.0.0.1:8000/demo in the browser using a GET request.

Observed result:
- The server crashes with a 500 error and the TypeError reported above when handling the GET request to a view that only defines an async POST handler.

Relevant APIs and symbols involved:
- django.views.View
- async post(request) method
- django.http.HttpResponse
- HttpResponseNotAllowed

problem_statement:
Accessing UserAdmin via to_field leads to link to PasswordResetForm being broken (404)

Description

(last modified by Simon Kern)

Accessing the UserAdmin via another model's Admin that has a reference to User (with to_field set, e.g., to_field="uuid") leads to the UserAdmin being accessed via a URL that looks similar to this one:
.../user/22222222-3333-4444-5555-666677778888/change/?_to_field=uuid

However the underlying form renders the password help text with a link whose target is filled in programmatically. The form defines a read-only password-hash field whose help text contains an anchor labeled "this form" and the href is produced by formatting a placeholder. In the form initializer, after delegating to the parent initializer, the code retrieves the password field and replaces the placeholder in the help text with a relative path that points one level up to "password/".

This results in the link to the PasswordResetForm being wrong when UserAdmin is accessed via a to_field URL, and thus ending up in a 404. If we drop the assumption that UserAdmin is always accessed via its primary key, the fix is to format the help-text link so it goes up two directory levels and then includes the user's primary key before "password/", i.e., construct a relative link that resolves to the correct password-reset path for the current user instance.

problem_statement:
Title
runserver with host 0's "Starting development server at <address>" doesn't work

Description

According to the tutorial, running the Django development server with the host set to 0 and port 8000 is intended to be the same as running it with the host set to 0.0.0.0 and port 8000. However, when I start the server using the short host notation and port 8000, the console output shows a watcher message and then:

Watching for file changes with StatReloader
...
Starting development server at http://0:8000/
...

This produces a URL with host "0", so you can't use that link in a browser. The output should display the URL with host 0.0.0.0 and port 8000 when the short host notation and port are provided on the command line, in order to stay consistent with the documentation.

problem_statement:
Sitemaps without items raise ValueError on callable lastmod.

Description

When a sitemap contains no items but supports returning lastmod for an item, it fails with a ValueError. The failure happens inside the sitemap implementation when get_latest_lastmod attempts to compute the maximum lastmod over all items; because the items sequence is empty, the max operation raises an error.

Exception Type: ValueError at /sitemap.xml
Exception Value: max() arg is an empty sequence

A possible solution is to change get_latest_lastmod so that:
- It first checks whether the sitemap object has a lastmod attribute; if it does not, it returns None.
- If lastmod is present and is a callable (i.e., a function that returns last modified dates for individual items), it attempts to compute the maximum of lastmod(item) for each item returned by items(). If computing that maximum raises either a TypeError or a ValueError (for example because the items sequence is empty), it returns None.
- If lastmod is present but not callable (i.e., it is a constant value), it simply returns that value.

This preserves the existing API surface (get_latest_lastmod, lastmod, items) while avoiding the empty-sequence error when no items are present.

problem_statement:
Title:
acreate(), aget_or_create(), and aupdate_or_create() doesn't work as intended on related managers.

Description

An async-compatible interface was added to QuerySet in commit 58b27e0dbb3d31ca1438790870b2b51ecdb10500. Unfortunately, that change also (unintentionally) added async acreate, aget_or_create, and aupdate_or_create methods to related managers. Moreover, those async methods do not call the corresponding create, get_or_create, and update_or_create methods on the related manager itself; instead, they call the QuerySet versions.

We should add proper async versions to related managers. The file to adjust is django/db/models/fields/related_descriptors.py. Note that related manager factories exist for different relationship types and directions, including forward and reverse variants, leading to multiple combinations that need handling.

Current problematic patterns observed in related manager factory implementations:

- In the reverse many-to-one manager factory, an async acreate method was implemented by wrapping the manager's create call with a sync-to-async adapter and the method's alters_data attribute was set. The synchronous get_or_create implementation in that factory checks the foreign-key value and injects the related instance into the kwargs by setting the foreign-key field name to the instance.

- In the forward many-to-many manager factory, an async acreate method was similarly implemented by wrapping the manager's create call with a sync-to-async adapter and setting the alters_data attribute. The synchronous get_or_create implementation accepts a through_defaults parameter and determines the database for writes by calling the router with the instance's class and the instance, then delegates to the appropriate DB-specific manager's get_or_create.

Because the async methods on related managers are currently delegating to QuerySet behavior rather than invoking the manager-specific logic (including ensuring the related FK is set and using the correct DB manager/through_defaults handling), they do not behave correctly for related managers. We need to implement proper async methods on related managers that mirror the manager-specific logic performed by their synchronous counterparts.

problem_statement:
Title: Strip unused annotations from count queries

Description

A queryset that annotates each Book with a count of its related chapters and then calls the count() method produces a SQL statement that includes the chapters-count annotation, despite that annotation not being used in any filter operations.

This produces the same result as calling count() directly on the Book queryset.

Django could be more intelligent about which annotations to include when building the SQL for a count() call on a queryset, stripping out any annotations that are not referenced by filters, other annotations, or ordering. This should speed up calls to count() when complex annotations are present.

There seems to be precedent for this behavior: related-object prefetching calls are ignored when performing count() queries.

I have also run into problems with QuerySet.count() being very slow on annotated query sets. Django uses a subquery for the count but injects a group by into the subquery. This typically causes the database server to deduplicate all matched rows using the group by columns which is, in general, extremely slow when there are a large number of matched rows. For example, consider the following model: class Person(models.Model): """Person model.""" first_name = models.TextField() last_name = models.TextField() country = models.TextField(null=True, blank=True) and query set: from django.db.models.functions import Concat from django.db.models import Value queryset = Person.objects.annotate(full_name=Concat('first_name', Value(' '), 'last_name')) queryset.count() generates the following query under PostgreSQL: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT "support_person"."id" AS Col1, CONCAT("support_person"."first_name", CONCAT(' ', "support_person"."last_name")) AS "full_name" FROM "support_person" GROUP BY "support_person"."id", CONCAT("support_person"."first_name", CONCAT(' ', "support_person"."last_name"))) subquery list(queryset) generates: SELECT "support_person"."id", "support_person"."first_name", "support_person"."last_name", "support_person"."country", CONCAT("support_person"."first_name", CONCAT(' ', "support_person"."last_name")) AS "full_name" FROM "support_person" I am not entirely sure why the subquery for the count needs to be any different from the query used when the query set itself is evaluated. There are some relevant comments in the source code here: ​https://github.com/django/django/blob/5deb7a86e8b54d052a3b1dbed1ae7142d362b1c5/django/db/models/sql/query.py#L404-L414 This has all been tested under Django 2.1.7.
This is somewhat related to #30158 where the compiler is not smart enough to determine if it can exclude subquery annotations from GROUP BY on aggregation.
The behaviour is actually a bit more bizarre than I thought. With the same person model, here are four count variations and the generated queries: 1. Person.objects.count() SELECT COUNT(*) AS "__count" FROM "people_person" 2. Person.objects.values('pk').count() SELECT COUNT(*) AS "__count" FROM "people_person" 3. Person.objects.annotate(full_name=Concat('first_name', Value(' '), 'last_name')).count() SELECT COUNT(*) FROM ( SELECT "people_person"."id" AS Col1, CONCAT("people_person"."first_name", CONCAT(' ', "people_person"."last_name")) AS "full_name" FROM "people_person" GROUP BY "people_person"."id", CONCAT("people_person"."first_name", CONCAT(' ', "people_person"."last_name")) ) subquery 4. Person.objects.annotate(full_name=Concat('first_name', Value(' '), 'last_name')).values('pk').count() SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT "people_person"."id" AS Col1 FROM "people_person") subquery So there's a simple workaround for the case I gave in my last comment in calling .values('pk') before .count(). However, that's not much help if Django or other libraries are the ones calling .count(). On the plus side, I have a better understanding of what the problem is from looking at the Django source code.
Just a note to say that the behaviour I was describing was rectified in ​https://github.com/django/django/pull/11062. The third case from above now executes the following SQL query: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM ( SELECT CONCAT("people_person"."first_name", CONCAT(' ', "people_person"."last_name")) AS "full_name" FROM "people_person" ) subquery Although the original ticket was about eliminating unneeded annotations completely, the result above is good enough for me, as the group by has been eliminated which was the real performance killer.

problem_statement:
Title: QuerySet.bulk_create() crashes on mixed case columns in unique_fields/update_fields

Description

Not sure exactly how to phrase this, but when I'm calling bulk_create on the manager for a model that has db_column set on fields, the generated SQL is invalid. Ellipses indicate other fields excluded for clarity.

The model maps Python field names to database column names and sets a custom database table name. For example, the model's table name is Activity_BlackListed, and there are fields where the Python name is blacklistid but the corresponding database column name is BlacklistID, and sectorid maps to SectorID, etc.

I call bulk_create on a queryset with update_conflicts set to true, and I pass update_fields containing the Python field name "sectorid" and unique_fields containing the Python field name "blacklistid".

The generated INSERT statement correctly uses the database column names (it inserts into the Activity_BlackListed table and lists the database column BlacklistID among the inserted columns). However, the generated ON CONFLICT clause incorrectly references the Python field names instead of the database column names, which leads to a syntax/runtime error from PostgreSQL.

PostgreSQL returns the following error message: ERROR: column "blacklistid" does not exist at character 1508

What should be generated is an ON CONFLICT clause that references the actual database column names (for example, BlacklistID for the conflict target and SectorID for the updated column), rather than the Python field names.

problem_statement:
UserCreationForm should save data from ManyToMany form fields
Description

When using the framework's built-in authentication user-creation form with a custom User model that defines many-to-many relationship fields, the data in all related form fields (for example, a model-based multiple-choice field that selects related instances) is not saved. This happens because, unlike its parent class (the framework's model form base class), the user-creation form's save method when called with the parameter commit=True omits calling the method that persists many-to-many relationships. This behavior was discussed on the django-developers mailing list https://groups.google.com/u/1/g/django-developers/c/2jj-ecoBwE4 and I'm ready to work on a PR.

Title: timesince raises TypeError with USE_TZ=True and >1 month interval

Description

(last modified by Sage Abdullah)

As of the referenced commit, calling the timesince utility with a datetime object that is one month (or more) in the past, while the USE_TZ setting is set to True, results in the following crash:
TypeError: can't subtract offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes

Test:
A test marked to require timezone support and run with USE_TZ set to True constructs a timezone-aware "now", creates a datetime 31 days earlier, and asserts that the human-readable timesince output for that earlier datetime is "1\xa0month".

Investigation:
I believe this is because the pivot datetime created at the linked location does not take into account the datetime object's tzinfo. Adding arguments to the pivot's datetime construction so that it uses the original object's tzinfo seems to fix the issue.

Happy to send a PR.

problem_statement:
Callable storage on FileField fails to deconstruct when it returns default_storage

Description

If the storage argument on a FileField is set to a callable that returns the default storage, the storage argument is omitted from the deconstructed form of the field instead of being included as a reference to the callable.

For example, consider a model setup where the module imports the framework's default storage and a filesystem storage, creates an alternate filesystem storage rooted at /media/other, and defines a function get_storage that randomly returns either the default storage or that alternate storage. A model is then defined with a FileField whose storage argument is set to that get_storage callable. Repeatedly running makemigrations against that model will randomly generate a migration that alternately includes or omits the storage argument that references the callable.

This case was overlooked in the fix for issue #31941. The deconstruct method checks whether the field's storage attribute is the default storage to decide whether to add the storage keyword argument, but at that point the field's storage attribute has already been evaluated. As a result, a callable that returns the default storage is treated as if the storage is the default and the storage argument is wrongly omitted instead of being recorded as a reference to the callable.

problem_statement:
After #26052 runserver returns response body for HTTP HEAD requests
Description
	
For compliance with RFC 2616, section 4.3, response bodies must not be returned for HEAD requests.
In #26052, the stripping of the response bodies was removed from Django in favour of letting the server perform the body removal, since the common servers (gunicorn, mod_wsgi etc) already do so.
However it appears that runserver does not strip the body, contrary to the timeline entry linked above.
As such, starting in Django 1.10 the responses from runserver for HEAD requests are no longer compliant with the spec. (In certain configurations this also results in "Broken pipe" error messages in runserver output, since compliant user agents expect to be able to terminate the connection after the headers are sent.)

STR:
1) Create a new virtual environment named "django-test".
2) Install Django with a version constraint that selects a release greater than 1.10 but less than 1.11.
3) Create a new Django project named "django-test" using the project creation utility.
4) Change into the new project's directory.
5) Start the development server using the project's management command to run the server.
6) In another terminal, issue an HTTP HEAD request against the local development server (for example, using a command-line HTTP client to send a HEAD request to 127.0.0.1:8000).
7) Observe the response returned by the client.

Expected:
HTTP/1.0 200 OK
Date: Fri, 07 Apr 2017 14:56:39 GMT
Server: WSGIServer/0.2 CPython/3.4.5
Content-Type: text/html
X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN

Actual:
The same HTTP response headers as above, but the response also contains the full HTML body of the default Django welcome page (the complete HTML document for the welcome page is returned), which should not be present for a HEAD response.

Tested with Python 2.7.13 and 3.4.5.
Doesn't reproduce under Django 1.9.13.

The spec says entity tag validators can still be set for HEAD requests: ​https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7232#section-2.4
Looks like another impetus for switching runserver to use another web server when feasible (#21978).
​PR #29343 was a duplicate.

problem_statement:
Formsets' add_fields() method fails in some circumstances if the argument index is None.

Description

Formsets' add_fields() method fails in some circumstances if the argument index is None. When a FormSet has the attributes self.can_delete == True and self.can_delete_extra == False, calling the add_fields() method on that FormSet fails if the argument index is None. This occurs for example when calling FormSet.empty_form(). The result is that the method raises the exception TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'NoneType' and 'int'.

In the Django source, there is a conditional that effectively checks whether deletion is enabled and then either whether deleting extra forms is allowed or whether the provided index is less than the initial form count. Because that conditional compares index to the initial form count without first ensuring index is not None, the comparison raises the TypeError when index is None. The fix would be to ensure the code checks that index is not None before comparing it to the initial form count.

How to Reproduce

A minimal reproduction creates a basic Django form with one character field, configures Django settings and setup, builds a formset factory for that form with deletion enabled and deletion of extra forms disabled, instantiates the formset with initial set to None, and then attempts to access the empty form. Accessing the empty form triggers add_fields() with index equal to None and raises the TypeError noted above.
